activity: Mrs. Caroline Vines and Mrs. Helen Holmes moving furniture into a Nissen hut on St. Paul's Road, Peterborough.

te.text:
MORE FURNITURE GOES INTO ARMY HUTS DESPITE QUIT NOTICES.

A policy of 'sit tight' and await developments has been adopted
by ex Servicemen who, with their wives and children, have moved
into unoccupied military huts in St. Paul's Road, Peterborough,
Northamptonshire, because they were unable to find other
accommodation as a result of the housing shortage. Notices to
quit have been served on some of the 'squatters', and German
prisoners have been brought in by the military authorities to
start pulling down huts on the site scheduled for demolition.
Among the families installed are Mr. and Mrs. Harry Joseph Vines
and their 3 1/2-year-old daughter Patricia. Mr. Vines, now an
inspector in a Diesel factory, is a former Petty Officer in the
Navy who won the British Empire Medal for bringing a lifeboat
safely to land after it had been 39 days in the Atlantic following
the torpedoing of a troopship. While recovering from his ordeal
in New York he met Caroline - now his wife, who comes from Brooklyn.
PHOTO SHOWS:- Mrs. Caroline Vines (second from right) assisted
by Mrs. Helen Holmes (on right), also in occupation of a hut, and
the children of other neighbours as she moves furniture into one
of the Nissen huts.
LUD August 9th 1946 PN.r.

activity: A Blue coat boy feeding a sow with her litter on the school farm at Horsham.

te.text:
LIFE AT THE BLUECOAT SCHOOL.

Christ's Hospital or "Blue Coat School", was founded by
Edward VI on the site of an old Greyfriars monastery, and down
to a few years ago was one of London's best known scholastic
institutions. It was pulled down to make room for extensions
of St. Bartholomew's Hospital and the new General Post Office,
in Newgate Street. The School is now carried on at HORSHAM in
an imposing building. Besides the usual subjects included in
any school curriculum, the boys are taught interesting things,
such as clay modelling, carpentry, weaving, spinning etc., and
have taken advantage of their move into the country by acquiring
a farm, the work on which is done by the boys. The school has
a band complete with mace bearer and this is a familiar sight
once a year in London when the school marches through the City to
their annual church service. The boys still wear the picturesque
costume of knee breeches, yellow stockings and blue coats.

O.P.S.  A Blue coat boy feeding a sow with her litter
         on the school farm at HORSHAM..  YHD/B. KEYSTONE.

activity: An artist's impression of a transatlantic flying boat base and composite aircraft in flight.

te.text:
MALINDINE. 4. 12. 35.

An artist's impression of
a Flying Base in the Atlantic.

FOR TRANSATLANTIC AIR SERVICE.—Secrets of the lead which Britain is giving
to commercial air development will be revealed at to-day's exhibition of wonderful
models which Imperial Airways are holding at the Science Museum, South Kensington.
This illustration by W. E. Truby, a "Daily Herald" artist, is inspired by the ambitious
transatlantic air scheme. The composite aircraft, seen in flight over a flying boat base,
is now being built by Messrs. Short Bros., for Imperial Airways. It consists of two
machines a small, high-speed monoplane with a heavy fuel and mail load and a huge
flying boat carrying practically no load. The small plane, unable to rise alone with its
heavy load, is lifted by the mother machine to a height of 10.000 feet and then launched
on its way.

Photograph.
Number Z3892
(TO BE QUOTED WHEN ORDERING)

activity: Three girls starting work selling men's shirts to retailers, dressed as commercial travellers in bowler hats.

te.text:
News
From EURO PUBLICITY LIMITED - 283a HIGH STREET - CROYDON - SURREY
Telephones : MUNicipal 3022/3/4 Telegrams : "EURO CROYDON"

RECEIVED
30 DEC 1963
D. H. EDITORIAL DEPT.

For Immediate Release
24th December, 1963.
Length - 200 words
Girls in Bowlers Sell Shirts
Three smart girls who hope to beat the men at their own
game have started work in a new job selling men's shirts to
retailers. They are the first of a team to be taken on by
Cornes and Company, 18, Finsbury Circus, London, E.C.2.
The girls have been fitted out for their parts as
commercial travellers and their appearance in the City is
expected to cause much comment.
From the left they are, Jean Radcliffe (19) of Watford
Way, Mill Hill; Anne Marchmont (21) of Upper Richmond Road, Sheen,
and Rosemary Dewhurst (19) of Sherwood Park Road, Mitcham.
All the girls have worked in the drapery trade.
They will also meet buyers at a party where the non-
creasing character of the product will be demonstrated by one of
the world's best exponents of Judo.
As an experiment which has never been tried before, the
venture is seen by Cornes & Co., as a new approach to selling.
"Many women have more tact and business ability than
men. If we find the experiment works as we think it will, more
girls will be taken on in other parts of the country," said
Leonard Steel, a director of Cornes.
- ends -

activity: Skipper DOUG EMERY of the cockle boat 'Sylvia May', using a short metal headed rake to work cockles out of the mud

te.text:
COCKLE TI ME
AT LEIGH ON SEA		DO/VIG

The humble cockle keeps the average Londoner
occupied for, at the most ten minutes, when
purchased by the saucer at the kerb-side- it keeps
the young and old of LEIGH ON SEA, busy however,
all the year round. There are other cockle grounds
around the English coasts, but Leigh claims to be
the biggest.
Leigh's fishing grounds bring out the family
boats in all seasons, and the succulent shell fish
are sieved, washed sorted and boiled, in sheds
down on the shore. The cockles are raked from
the mud at low tide, and the boats are out at the
ground, perhaps for 12 hours at a stretch.

PHOTO SHOWS:- Skipper DOUG EMERY of the cockle
boat "Sylvia May", uses a short metal headed rake to
work cockles out of the mud. It's no joke with the
cold weather coming on.

activity: Smoke rising from the hull of the battleship H.M.S. Rodney during shipbreaking operations at T. Ward's scrapyard in Inverkeithing, Scotland.

te.text:
"GRAVEYARD OF GIANTS"
WHERE BATTLESHIPS GO FOR SCRAP    DG/PR

"Abandon Hope All Ye That Enter Here" is the ironic
warning over the entrance to the jetty of Messrs.
Thomas Ward, shipbreakers, of Inverkeithing,
Scotland, and so far as warships are concerned, the
phrase applies down to the last rivet.
Wards are the biggest shipbreakers in Britain, and
one of the largest in the world,  Not only are they
the biggest shipbreakers, but they break up the
biggest ships.  To their yards and to others
such as Metal Industries, or Arnott and Young's-
come such floating giants as "Rodney", "Revenge",
"Renown"; the "New York", once Hitler's "strength
through joy" liner, and many others.  Mighty fighting
ships which sailed triumphantly through two world
wars, find their last resting place under scrapyard
cranes.  Guns which the combined fleets of
the Third Reich and Imperial Japanese Navy, failed
to muzzle, are silent as hissing oxy-acetylene
cutters carve into their vitals.
Much of the valuable scrap goes to sea again in
the form of new ships, and thus fights in Britain's
export drive.  Brass, copper and much needed alloys
are sent to Sheffield, while metal scrap goes to
Newcastle.

PHOTO SHOWS:- Smoke rises in a black pall over the
hull of H.M.S. Rodney, at T. Ward's scrapyard.
Rodney has been broken up in 16 months and the
remaining oil and sludge in her double-bottoms
is burned out to continue the cutting operations.
FOX PHOTOS  MMH

THIS PHOTOGRAPH
has not been submitted
to EVENING PAPERS

activity: Miss Mollie Taylor, a glass-eye maker, blowing a piece of glass tubing into shape in a workshop.

te.text:
2442)      SHE MAKES "EYES" FOR A LIVING

A brother and sister, aged 20 and 22 respectively are
now carrying on a trade which has been in the family
for nearly a century - that of specialists in the
difficult art of making glass eyes. They are Miss
Mollie and Mr. Gus Taylor, who with the aid of a
Bunsen Burner, tubes of coloured glass, strong lungs,
and above all, artistic talent, sit in their West
End workshop supplying the demand which comes from
all over the world for their particular produce. In
addition to making glass eyes for living persons, the
Taylors make them for a number of figures at Madame
Tussauds, Mr. Gus Taylor having made the eyes for the
figure of the Duchess of Kent. A glass eye takes about
half-an-hour to make.

Photo shows :- MISS MOLLIE TAYLOR, who is the youngest
woman glass-eye maker in the world, blowing a
piece of glass tubing into shape in their West End shop.

24/2/36      C          (Topical Press)

MAKING EYES.—Miss Mollie
Taylor, probably the youngest
woman glass-eye maker in the world,
blowing a glass tube into shape at a
London workshop. Her family have
been glass-eye makers for nearly a
century.

te.text:
PROPERTY OF

REC. 2 - MAY 1951

THE OLDEST OF THEM ALL.

GK/7262-14.  The man who is not too old at 84.  John Beddow, 
has been working since he was 14 full time, before that he 
worked half time from the age of 10, earning 1/1d. a week. 
Like the other men he is now paid the basic rate for the job 
he does.  His money averages £4 a week.

THE OLD FOLK OF INDUSTRY

GK/7262.  Seeking to prove a man is "not too old at 70"
is the engineering firm of Rubery, Owen and Co. of Darlaston,
Staffs who have started an "Old Folks Workshop" which they
call "Sons of Rest".  Situated about a mile away from the
noise and bustle of the main factory, twelve men, all over
the age of 70 work on their own with no young workers beside
them to give them an inferiority complex over their ages.
The veterans start an hour later than the main factory.  They
do drilling and assembly work on office equipment and farm
implements for overseas markets.  The experiment has been
going on for 10 months and has proved a great success. Doctors
who are urging more active employment for elderly people for
the benefit of their health support it.  It is also a means
of saving for industry skilled hands vitally necessary these
days, which would otherwise be lying idle.

activity: surface at Rawdon Colliery after the container winding system had been introduced

te.text:
RAWDON COLLIERY.

Rawdon Colliery, which is on the border of
Derbyshire and Leicestershire, is now one of the most
efficient collieries in the country. Before 1952
success in improving output had reached a stage where it
was not possible to get more coal out of the pit without
reorganising the shafts for higher capacity. An
entirely new method of overcoming this difficulty, whilst
avoiding delays and consequent loss of output, was
conceived by the former Area General Manager,
Mr. J.J.Torrance, and his Chief Engineer, Mr. F.Ashley.
They scrapped all the complicated and orthodox methods
of collecting the coal and installed an automatic system
employing six movable containers, each holding 4 tons,
to replace tubs used for winding up the shaft. These
containers, which are moved on rollers in and out of the
winding cage, are filled from a bunker at pit-bottom, and
are wound and emptied at high speed, only one man con-
trolling the operation on the surface.

Winding now takes place in one shaft instead of two,
and the six containers replace 650 tubs formerly used for
winding the output up the shafts.

The reorganisation has reduced the number of men
employed from 114 to 16, and improved the capacity of the
Rawdon shaft from 148 to 360 tons an hour

CROWN COPYRIGHT RESERVED.  MINISTRY OF HOUSING & LOCAL GOVERNMENT.
Four prototype houses built for the Sheffield City Council by the
Public Works Department under the 5M system of construction devised
by the Research and Development Group of the Ministry of Housing
and Local Government.  This system, which marks a new attempt to
bring the advantages of industrialisation into the field of house-
building, has been derived from the 5M CLASP system used at
Stevenage for a group of old people's flatlets.  The new system
is called 5M, because as at Stevenage, it is based upon a planning
grid of 1' 8" (5 x the module of 4").  The object has been to
modify the CLASP system which has been shown to have advantages in
the reduction of site labour and building time, to suit the
performance standards, and the levels of cost, of 2-storey housing.

Ministry of Housing & Local Government.           January, 1963

te.text:
CALCRAFT   ILLUS.                 8.12.42
SADLER'S WELLS BALLET
The present season at the New Theatre ends on
December 19th. The company then go to York (Theatre
Royal) where they open on Christmas Eve. They go on
to the Prince's Theatre, Bradford, from January 4th
to 9th, and after a holiday, return to the New
Theatre on January 25th.
THE BIRDS
The choregrapher is Robert Helpmann, who has set this
his third ballet to the music of Respighi. The
detting and dresses are by a Chinese artist, Chiang Yee.
The ballet was first presented at the New Theatre on
November 24th, and will be in the repertoire of the
Company when they are in Yorkshire.
THE SYNOPSIS
There is no bird in the garden that pleases the
melancholy Dove, least of all the Hen who makes
ludicrous advances to him. Not until he meets the
simple Nightingale does he fall in love. Unfortunately
his feelings are shared by the jealous and pompous
Cuckoo (who has quarrelled with both the hen and the
Sparrows). In a despairing effort to gain their
amours, the Cuckoo disguises himself as the Dove, while
the Hen disguises herself as the Nightingale. No
one is deceived by the disguise except the two
impostors, who fall happily into each other's arms.
But they are quickly unmasked by the mischievous
Sparrows. They leave after an angry scene and the
Sparrows prepare the way for the wedding of the Dove
and the Nightingale.
1. The Dove (Alexis Rasine) and the Nightingale
(Beryl Grey).

te.text:
"IGLOOS" ON A KENT FARM

Fourteen "IGLOOS" - small tents constructed
with a rigid tubular steel skeleton, have made their
appearance at TEMPLE FARM, DARTFORD MARSHES, KENT.
This is from an idea of the farmer - MR. FRED
BARKER, and it now enables his workers, both casual and
regular, to work even in the bad weather.
Normally, when it rains and there is no
inside work most workers are "stood off". On MR. BARKER'S
farm there is now full employment at all times.
It also helps him to get his crops picked
at the right time. For instance, radishes must come out
not a day later than three weeks after sowing.
PICTURE SHOWS:

CASUAL WORKERS PICKING RADISHES
IN THE RAIN THIS MORNING. WHEN
HOEING, THE CONTRAPTION IS LIFTED
AND DRAGGED AFTER THEM. FRONT
FORKS ARE PUSHED INTO THE GROUND FOR
STABILITY IN WIND.
56625 4/6/56 JOHN TOPHAM

TOPHAM, LTD.
20, MAIN ROAD,
SIDCUP,
KENT.

PROPERTY OF

activity: representation of a Caribbean settlement and the 'House in the Sun' in the Grand Hall at the Daily Mail Ideal Home Exhibition at Olympia

te.text:
AN ILLUSTRATION from
THE DAILY MAIL IDEAL HOME EXHIBITION
OLYMPIA, MARCH 6—MARCH 31 1962
WITH COMPLIMENTS—NO FEE is required for reproduction of this picture if it is published as news
of THE IDEAL HOME EXHIBITION at Olympia, or in conjunction with an article about this exhibition
PATRICK MURPHY, The Press Representative.

6195
The vast space of the Grand Hall, permeated with light and warmth, is a repre-
sentation of a Caribbean settlement by the sea. From the entrance, visitors
will see the House in the Sun, a beautiful white modern structure which is
both a suntrap and sun shield. From the "hills" behind a waterfall passes
beneath the house before sliding away. The interior of the House is as
beguiling as its outward appearance. The living room is furnished to the
tastes of Sir Malcolm Sargent; the electronic bedroom by Stirling Moss and
the kitchen by Mrs. John Profumo - actress Valerie Hobson. Approaching this
House from the Main Entrance, visitors will pass through lines of colourful
stands garlanded with flowers. Towering 50 ft. above the stands, four Apamate
trees fill the vast space with their huge canopies of variegated foliage.
O.P.S. The bedroom designed by Stirling Moss. Entirely electronic, it is
modelled on the bedroom he is building for himself in his new home in
Shepherds Market.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
- 6 MAR 1962
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

press release 840
EMBARGO: 20/9/63, 12 NOON
HOUSING DEVELOPMENT & CONSTRUCTION LTD.
PROTOTYPE HOUSES BUILT IN THREE WEEKS
The prototype of a new system of industrialised house
building has just been completed by Housing Development &
Construction Ltd., at Stratford-upon-Avon. It is a pair of
semi-detached, three bedroomed houses, designed and built to
the full Parker-Morris Committee Recommendations, and to the
specification of the local authority Stratford-upon-Avon M.B.
It only required three weeks of normal working with a very
small team of men to complete this pair of houses for occupation.
This is undoubtedly the fastest erection time of any system
of truly permanent housing for local authorities yet developed.
The 16 ft. x 12 ft. living room of the centrally heated
H.D.C. house is separated from the dining and kitchen
area by a glazed screen - just one of several alternatives.
All walls and ceiling have an unusually high degree of heat
insulation.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
20 SEP 1963
PLEASE RETURN
TO

THREE FAMILIES SHARE THIS BATHROOM.

Eastbourne, Eng: Three families in the bathroom 
they share in a former institution in the grounds

KENT OATS ARE SPROUTING IN THE FIELDS
---
This picture, from Green Street Green, near
Dartford, Kent, shows a sample of oats which have
fallen from the stooks - which have been standing for
the last few weeks unable to be carried in because of
the weather. Grain has fallen from the shells and
has sprouted and taken root.

if the corn is not collected soon it will be a total

 Firemen and other rescue workers,

Parents search debris 
 for their 
 children 
 By Paul Hopkins 
 THE kids around Nether- 
 ton-road loved their 
 house of make-believe. No 
 furniture to be careful about, 
 no carpets to dirty, no-one to 
 tell them to be quiet. 
 ... Even then firemen, police and 
 a number of parents - uncertain 
 how many children had been 
 playing there - went on hunting 
 with the aid of searchlights until 
 they were sure all the playmates 
 were safe. 
 One of the children who ran 
 to safety was nine-year-old 
 Carol Fry, of Netherton-street. 
 The other boys were 10-year- 
 old Stephen Hamilton, of 
 Tewkesbury-road, Tottenham, 
 and brothers Brian O'Gorman, 
 aged six, and David, aged nine, 
 of Netherton-road. 
 ... Beneath the debris one of the 
 five was trapped. Eleven-year-old 
 Kenneth Adams, of Seven 
 Sisters-road, had not run fast 
 enough.

te.text:
166182 LUD
AMERICA IMPORTING BRITISH-MADE FERGUSON TRACTORS.
£15,000,000 ORDER.
Coventry, Eng: In the world's largest tractor factory
operated by multi-millionaire Harry Ferguson here,
250 tractors leave the production lines every day as
part of a £15,000,000 order for America - one of the
greatest manufacturers of these machines.
First batch of this order - vital part of Britain's
export drive - will sail in the freighter 'American
Farmer', recently salvaged off British coasts when
sailing here with essential parts for the tractors.
The machines, selling to the States at £372 each, are
made at the Coventry plant leased by the 63-year-old
Ferguson, who recently returned from America to live
at his Cotswold home.
PHOTO SHOWS: Newly-completed Ferguson tractors are
driven to their place in the 'export line' -
machines waiting shipment to America at the Coventry
factory.
January 16th 1948 PN.g. List 1.

TURNING GOLD INTO BOOKS.

In spite of thousands of years of scientific research
a machine has not yet been invented to beat gold, with
the delicate manipulation which is essential to success,
and so the job is still carried on by hand, in almost
the same way as it was carried on in the time of Queen
Cleopatra, varying only in the fact that  a bronze hammer
was used by the ancients in place of the steel one used
today, and that machinery forms a small part of the
early stages..
O.P.S.  Gold beaters at work, for hours on end these
        men beat away with their hammers until the
        squares and ribbons of gold are in leaves, only

te.text:
D.H. White.           5.11.47.

Fishing for coal in the Leeds-Liverpool
canal at Adlington, Lancs. (See story).

19. Robert Davis hands in his home made
    cage with coal in.

FISHING FOR COAL IN THE LEEDS-LIVERPOOL, CANAL.
The Leeds-Liverpool canal at Chorley, Lancs,
is almost dry-just a little water in the middle
of masses of mud.
Seventy-three-years-old Jimmy Blundell, who sailed
that canal as captain of the barge for almost 50
years and his pal Bob Davis, aged 66, another ex-barge
skipper, remembered that coal fell out of the barges
into the canal.
So Jimmy and Bob made a metal dredge. It pulls up
broken bottles and stones but coal too.
The two ex-captains are working their way along the
canal and average two bags of coal every afternoon.
OPS. Robert Davis hands in his home made cage with
coal in.

of the usual five minutes in radiant heat of 300 cent.
() Jim Townley, one of the tailors at  rankensteins

te.text: g a silk stocking length as it leaves the

Making Silk Stockings.
In an old workhouse which has been converted
into a factory, between 25,000 and 30,000 dozen
pairs of nylon, pure silk and rayon stockings
are being produced each week.
Most of the stockings made in this factory are
non-fashioned. They are made on a circular
machine and the mock fashioning marks and seams
are added after they come off.
Fully fashioned stockings are knitted flat and seams
are joined afterwards.
The entire output of fully fashioned nylon stockings
and a considerable quantity of mock fashioned
stockings made in this factory are all for
export.

OPS. The stockings are put on to a moving belt of flat
metal "legs" to be shaped before it is sprayed with
water.

activity: Massey-Harris No.21, 12 foot cut combine harvester gathering wheat on land formerly requisitioned for military use

te.text:
The rapid expansion of allied air forces during the war resulted in
aerodromes sprawling across some of Britain's best agricultural land.  When
the planes finally departed, this requisitioned land, covered with runways,
perimeter tracks and military installations, was left neglected.

Co-Partnership Farms Ltd of Boreham, Essex, lost some of their best
land in this way and it was only recently handed back to them.  They immed-
iately commenced clearing all traces of military occupation so that the land
could be prepared for cropping as soon as possible.

The results of this work can be seen in the picture which shows a
Massey-Harris No.21, 12 foot cut combine harvester gathering wheat at one
hundred quarters a day from two hundred and seventy acres of land that had been
under military occupation for more than six years.

It is essential under present conditions that all land be brought back
into production as quickly as possible.  It says much for individual industry
that not only has it brought this war neglected land back into good heart, but
is using the most modern means to harvest the crops which are the result of
their initiative and labour.


Co-Partnership Farms Ltd
Boreham,           Chelmsford
(No Fee or Acknowledgement required)

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE 
'DAILY HERALD' ART LIBRARY 
AND MUST BE RETURNED

activity: Friends and caravan dwellers restraining and forcing back bailiffs during an eviction attempt at a site in Chertsey-lane, Egham.

te.text:
PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
16 OCT 1958
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

Friends restrain one of the
caravan dwellers. The
[illegible]
are seen centre one wearing a mac
the other wearing a homberg

Two bailiffs—in homburg and coat—are forced back.
72 FAMILIES
FORCE OUT
THE BAILIFFS
FOUR bailiffs who went to
clear 72 families from
their homes on a caravan site
had to retreat yesterday be-
fore they could serve one
eviction notice.
A mass of angry men and
women linked arms and forced
the bailiffs off the site.
Then the caravaners blocked
entrances to the site with an old
caravan and two old cars.
Today they will be ready to
carry on the fight for their
homes.
The families live in Chertsey-
lane, Egham, Surrey. The local
council has told them they must
go because the site is in the
Green Belt area. An extension
of their notice-to-quite ended
yesterday.
A TRUCE
When the bailiffs first arrived
a two-hour "truce" was agreed
while a deputation from the
site went to No. 10, Downing-
street.
They were told the Prime
Minister could not intervene. At
the Ministry of Housing they
got the same answer.
The deputation returned and
the bailiffs tried to move in.
Within ten minutes they were
back on the road.
They told the caravaners:
" We will be back."
The families have been offered
temporary accommodation and
later Army huts as homes in
Godalming. But they refuse to
leave...

te.text:
PROPERTY OF 
 DAILY HERALD 
 RCD. 18 FEB 1954 
 PLEASE RETURN 
 TO 
 ART LIBRARY

LONDON BUREAU 
 LN 266266 DAW 
 SHIP BEING BUILT IN UNFINISHED DRY DOCK 
 UNDER-COVER BUILDING 
 NEWPORT, MON: The first British shipyard in 
 which vessels are being built in dry dock and 
 under cover is somewhat unique in that work 
 is being carried out on the first of two 3,000 
 ton ships while the dock itself is in the process 
 of construction. Thus, as the size of the ship 
 grows, so will the dock. If everything goes 
 according to plan, they will, by the time the ship 
 is built, be able to open the dock gate and allow 
 the vessel to float out on the 40 ft. tide. 
 The dock, which was opened in November by 
 Sir David Maxwell Fyfe, Home Secretary and Minister 
 for Welsh Affairs, is situated at the mouth of the 
 River Usk. The two ships ordered are both wood 
 pulp carriers for a Canadian company, and sections 
 of them, after being prefabricated in a number of 
 shops, are lowered into position in the dock. 
 PHOTO SHOWS:- In the large new workshop at the dock, 
 sections of the first Canadian ship are assembled 
 together. 
 17th February 1954 PN-b

activity: the features and development of the Gillette Techmatic razor

te.text:
SOME THINGS, like raw gold and racehorses, improve with handling. The
same isn't true of razor blades. In fact, the more you handle a blade, the
tougher your shaving task is likely to become. Even removing it carelessly
from the paper wrapper can badly bruise the cutting edge.
Which is why those mag-
nificent men who design
shaving machines have at
last come up with a super-
swift invention that does
away with the need for any-
one ever to touch a razor
blade again.
The new Techmatic razor,
developed by Gillette, offers all
the close-shave advantages of
the traditional razor while
eliminating completely the
chore of gingerly switching
blades.
Like all the best inventions,
the idea behind it is a simple
one, similar to the cartridge-
loading of a camera.
FLICK
In effect, the Techmatic
presents the shaver with a
slender 10in.-long razor blade,
safely coiled inside a plastic
clip-on cartridge.
The actual length of shaving
edge exposed to the chin is the
same as in the normal razor.
But as the edge becomes dulled
you merely flick a lever to wind
in the next razor-sharp section.
A numbered window at the
back of the razor tells you how
many edges you have used up,
and since the coil is irrever-
sible there is no danger of
going back to a previously used
edge.
When the entire 10in. coil
has been wound through the
streamlined razor-head you buy
a new clip-on cartridge and
start again.
At the moment, unless you
live in the London television
area, the Techmatic is a
machine that money can't buy.
The razor, which sells at £2 2s.,
has been given a highly suc-
cessful trial run in the capital,
where the refill cartridges are
now available at 8s. 11d. each.
'The Techmatic will be
by WILLIAM SPICER
introduced nationwide. We
anticipate a heavy demand
since the Techmatic is the
very last word in shaving com-
fort,' says Vivian Burchill,
group brand manager.
'We reckon that the aver-
age shaver will only need to
buy new Techmatic cartridges
four or five times a year. One
Techmatic edge lasts as long as
a double-edged blade.'
Perhaps the big break-
through that really short-
circuited the electric shaver
men was the discovery that
stainless-steel razor blades
could be vastly improved by
giving them a coating of very
special plastic.
This process, invented and
patented by Gillette, has re-
moved the drag from shaving.
SLICE
'Imagine the bristles on
your chin as small saplings
and the razor blade as an axe,'
says Peter Williams, Gillette's
head of development.
'In the old days, the axe
would cut half-way through
each sapling and then have to
be tugged the rest of the way.
In some mysterious way, the
new plastic coating enables the
blade to slice through sapling
after sapling with absolutely
no sign of tug. We know what
it does, but I have to admit
that we don't yet understand
how.'
The miracle coating—a solid
fluorocarbon polymer similar
to the chemical applied to non-
stick frying pans—stubbornly
refuses to give up its secrets.
'You might call it a lucky
discovery,' says Peter Williams.
'But it came as the result of
painstaking research.'
Gillette have mastered the
secret of making this micro-
scopically thin film behave on
the edge of their Super Silver
blades. And naturally the
technique is thrown in as an
'extra' with the new con-
veyor-belt Techmatic.

activity: Mrs. Cropp and children at the door of their "home", a wooden fruit picker's hut on Wested Farm.

te.text:
PROBLEM OF A WOMAN AND SIX CHILDREN
---
Living in one room - a wooden fruit picker's
hut, on Wested Farm, Crockenhill, near Swanley,
Kent, is Mrs. May Cropp, her three children and a
further three granchildren (offspring of one of her
daughters).
She is a squatter.  There is no sanitation
anywhere near the hut - nor the usual amenites.  The
hut leaks, is unsanitary, and is certainly not
weatherproof.
How she came to be there does not matter - what
does matter is that she cannot get another home to
live - and owing to the bad state of affairs the
farmer, C.T. Miller, of Wested Farm, has asked the
police to evict them in the hope that they will
be found better accomodation.
As it is, the children - ranging from a few
months to six years - cannot possibly be properly
fed, clothed and educated - and there is no talk of
them going regularly to school.
In this cold weather, some of them are to
be seen playing in the mud around their "home".
The Dartford Rural District Council, under
whose jurisdiction their "home" comes, should look
into the matter - the farmer is certainly not to
[illegible] the best housing he can offer - even
2.  Mrs. Cropp and children at the door of their
"home".
19836      4/12/46      John Topham, Sidcup, Kent.

Dec 19th 1966 PAP 125712-1 (PNR-G)

AMERICA ORDERS MORE JETSTREAMS

The first prototype HP 137 JETSTREAM, an
executive and local-service aircraft,
under construction at the Handley Page
works at Radlett, Hertfordshire.
Now, five months before the plane's first
flight, it is announced that America has
placed an order for an additional 65

have been ordered by K.R. Cravens Corporation
of St. Louis, Missouri, through its wholly-
owned subsidiary International Jetstream
Corporation. This is an addition to an
order placed earlier this year.
Jetstreams, powered by prop-jet engines, are
able to use small grass fields, cruise at
over 300 mph, fly at 30,000 ft., and have
a range of 2,000 miles.
The first prototype is due to fly next Spring.

activity: Angry villagers demanding the demolition of a new block of council flats in Croft, Leicestershire, which they describe as looking like a prison.

te.text:
ANGRY VILLAGERS are to demand that a new block of 
council flats should be pulled down. They claim the block 
looks just like a prison. 
“It’s an absolute monstrosity,” one villager said 
last night. “If a private builder dared to build 
such a thing the council would be the first to 
object.” 
The £30,000 flats at 
Croft, Leics, are being 
built of concrete sections. 
Work on them is almost 
finished. 
But the villagers want all 
work on the “prison” to stop. 
Their parish council have 
asked Blaby Rural Council to 
meet a village deputation as 
soon as possible to hear 
demands for the demolition 
of the building. 
EYESORE 
Yesterday Mr. Don Wood, 
who lives opposite the flats 
in Broughton Road, Croft, 
said: “If the council had set 
out to create an eyesore 
deliberately they could not 
have done a better job.” 
Another Broughton Road 
resident, Mr. Ian Woollard, 
declared: “If we fail to get 
satisfaction we shall go to 
the Ministry of Housing and 
Local Government.” 
His neighbour, Mr. Charles 
Saxton, added: “Someone 
has made an almighty mis- 
take in putting up this mon- 
strosity. It must come 
down.” 
Mr. Thomas Heap, Clerk of 
Blaby Rural Council, said: 
“These are the first flats of 
this type we have erected. 
We didn’t expect this 
uproar.”

SUN 
 PROPERTY 
 15 JUL 1966 
 Please return to 
 ART LIBRARY

activity: oil-burning boilers at the new Bankside Power Station starting to supply electricity.

te.text:
244479         SKI
BANKSIDE POWER STATION STARTS PRODUCTION.

London:    A battery of 12 oil-burning boilers at
the new and controversial Bankside Power Station,
at which the first 60,000-kilowatt turbo-alternator,
of about 80,000 horse-power, has just started to
supply electricity.
One of the conditions under which the power station
was allowed laid down that oil and not coal was to
be burned. Other conditions were that the building
was approved by the Royal Fine Arts Commission, and
that the building must be set back far enough from
the Thames not to interfere with the projected road
and promenade. The protests about the building
came from the London County Council, the City Council,
and the Southwark Council, from the Dean and
Chapter of St. Paul's Cathedral - the planned power
station was opposite to St. Paul's, on the other side
of the river - and from such bodies as the Society
for the Protection of Ancient Buildings. Opposition
became so strong that in January 1947 a public
inquiry was held. The Government, however, allowed
the building, provided that the conditions were
observed.
When completed the station will comprise four
60,000-kilowatt generating sets, when the oil
consumption at full load, 16-hours a day, will be 67
tons an hour, consuming (in one winter's day) about
850 tons.
January 20th. 1953.   PN-h

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
21 JAN 1953
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

Nantgarw Colliery, first on the list of
Wales new modern collieries.
The first coal face of the developed
colliery at Nantgarw, between Cardiff and
Pontypridd is now being opened out for
horizon mining, and production is due to
commence in July.
OPS. Dai Jones, maintenance fitter from
Porth has been at Nantgarw for over three
years. He is pictured preparing a
neumatic boring machine, ready to go
underground.
In contrast to the old hand operated
borers, these new machines, carrying up to
three boring heads, are instantly adjusted
to any height and angle. They cut into
rock without effort.  In the foreground
are lumps of blue pennant stone which have
been bored like butter in tests.

activity: discovery of the body of a deceased male infant on a railway line

te.text:
At 6.25a.m. on 27th May, the dead body of a baby
boy aged about 1 month, well nourished was found
on the Southern Railway line between Barnes
Common and Putney.
The body was clad in a white knitted vest. There
were many injuries to the body, and burns as a result
of coming into [crossed out] contact with the conductor
rail, which suggests it had been thrown from a
train proceeding towards Waterloo. The child was
well developed, with fair hair and blue eyes.
The police are anxious to trace any person
travelling between Barnes and Putney between 9.30
and 1 a.m. 27th May, who might have seen anything
dropped from a carriage window, or who has any
knowledge of a male child of his age being missing
from its accustomed place.

Mrs MARGUERITE EASTWOOD (committed)
sentenced to death for the
murder of the baby.

activity: A farm worker and his employer chatting over a garden gate in front of a newly built house.

te.text:
PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
EDITORIAL
LIBRARY

The house
that LEONARD
built ...
FARM-WORKER Leonard
Algar claims a housing
record of his own.
In the little village of Carl-
ton Colville, near Lowestoft,
stands a well-built house, with
three bedrooms, three rooms
downstairs, bathroom, elec-
tricity, hot and cold water, and
three-quarters of an acre of
garden.
Built more than fourteen
months ago, this house is be-
lieved to be the first to be
erected under the Govern-
ment's scheme which helps
farm workers to have houses
built for themselves on their
own land.
His employer, Farmer Stan-
ley Newson, of Grove Farm,
told me about it. "Leonard
bought the land, had the house
built, and got married," he
said. "I think a lot of farm
workers would do the same if
they knew that the facilities
were available."
What are these facilities?
Up to 85 per cent. of the total
cost of building a house can be
borrowed at the rate of 3 1/2 per
cent. interest, repayable within
30 years.
For example, if the house
cost £1,100 (the price Leonard
paid for his) as much as £935
could be borrowed, if necessary.
The cost of interest and re-
payment over this period would
then average less than £1 per
week, and less still, of course,
if the sum borrowed were
smaller.
The scheme also provides an
annual grant, increased by the
Labour Government to £15 for
40 years, a total of £600, for all
such houses occupied by farm
workers.
And no development charges
are made where these houses
are concerned.
The first step for a farm
worker to take is to apply to
the clerk of his rural district
council. Those councils that
administer the Small Dwellings
Acquisition Act, which deals
with this matter, should pro-
perly give priority in the grant-
ing of building licences to men
working on the land.
The farm worker who is a
member will find that his
union is always ready to help
him deal with the formalities.
B. A. Steward
The kitchen—light, modern,
well-equipped.
Over their own front gate the
Algars chat with Farmer
Newson.

A "gold Rush" has started in Sheffield, where the firm of F.J
Brindley Ltd., of Pond Street, are working day and night to

activity: An official from the St Pancras Housing department posting requisitioning notices on the door of No. 5 Houghton Place.

te.text:
Mr. O'LEARY WINS HIS HOME BACK
" Herald " Reporter
HERE is the cameraman's view of the closing stages of the Battle of the Second Floor Back, which ended yesterday at Houghton-place, N.W., in victory for the tenant.
The battle began six weeks ago when Mr. Charles O'Leary was evicted from the single room sublet to him by Mrs. Eliades after a Tribunal had reduced his rent from £2 10s. to 17s. 6d.
Three days ago St. Pancras Borough Council requisitioned the room—but a new lock on the street door kept Mr. O'Leary and his wife out.
So the Town Clerk, acting under the powers recently given by Mr. Bevan, requisitioned the whole house.
When Mr. O'Leary and council officials went along yesterday to take possession they found the front door open—but there was a new lock on the door of his flat.
" Break it open," said the Housing Manager to the council's joiner—and here you see him doing it, with Mr. O'Leary looking on. The other picture shows an official posting up the requisitioning notice.
Within a few minutes the lock had been replaced by another and two keys given to Mr. O'Leary.
Said the Housing Manager: " I'm notifying Mrs. Eliades that she and her tenants are now our tenants; that she now has no right to deny any tenant access to this house and that she must obey the Council."
Mr. O'Leary says he is suing Mrs. Eliades for loss of six weeks' wages—" about £60."
" I'd to give up my job as a chef to take time off to fight this case," he told me. " I've been separated from my wife, who had to take a ' sleeping-in ' job in a hospital and I have had to sleep in lodging-houses. For a few days after we were turned out we had to live in a work-house."

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

activity: Norman Cornish, a coal hewer and artist, standing with his portrait of his grandmother at the 'Art by the Miner' exhibition at the Academy Cinema.

te.text:
THE "OTHER LIFE"
OF NORMAN
CORNISH, MINER
SINCE he was 14, Norman
Cornish—he is only 28
now—has led two lives.
One has been spent in the
Dean and Chapter Colliery,
Durham, where he earns his
living as a coal-hewer.
The other has been spent with
brushes and canvas in his free
time, recording with steadily in-
creasing mastery of form and
colour the men and the women
and the grim grandeur of the
world of coal.
And now, along with other
miners who fill their leisure time
with the colour they never see at
work, he is exhibiting his paint-
ings in London.
Norman was taught to draw
and paint at the Spennymoor
Settlement. Five of his paint-
ings in the present exhibition
have been bought by the Na-
tional Coal Board, which
sponsors the show.
Outstanding is his portrait of
his grandmother—he is standing
by it in this "Daily Herald"
photograph. "She's grand," he
says.
This exhibition covers many
artistic activities besides paint-
ing. There are ship models,
carvings, model aircraft, work-
ing models of mines, violins,
pipes, table-linen and shawls. .
"Art and the Miner" is on
view at the Academy Cinema,
Oxford-street, W. It opens today
from 10 a.m. to 10 p.m. (Sundays
2 p.m. to 10 p.m.) and closes
November 2. Admission is free.

Copyright
Photo
BY F. GREAVES.
NUMBER

ART BY THE MINER EXHIBITION.
N.S. Cornish a coal hewer from Dean and Chapter

which is exhibited at the Art by the Miner exhibition
which opened at the Academy Cinema today.

FIRST PUBLICATION MONDAY'S DAILIES 13.5.46.
THREE IN FOUR NEW BRITISH LOCOMOTIVES GO OVERSEAS
Seventy-five per cent of the output of new locomotives by the
North British Locomotive Company of Glasgow is going overseas.
Current orders include 150 for S.Africa, 110 for India and 40
for Malaya; orders for the home market include 100 for the LNER
aspart of a larger consignment. Six years of practically no
replacements enable the works to look forward to a long period
of activity, and view of the pressure of work the firm is to
recruit several hundred apprentices. The picture shows:

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION WEDNESDAY'S DAILIES... 19TH AUGUST, 1959.
NEW TECHNIQUES IN BRITISH SHIP CONSTRUCTION.
LE. 19TH AUGUST, 1959.
WORK IS NOW WELL ADVANCED ON THE LARGEST ALL-WELDED ALUMINIUM
SUPERSTRUCTURE YET BUILT INTO A BRITISH SHIP, THE 40,000 TON
ORIENT LINER, "ORIANA", AT PRESENT UNDER CONSTRUCTION IN THE
VAST YARDS OF THE FAMOUS BUILDERS, VICKERS ARMSTRONG, BARROW-
IN-FURNESS, SHE IS DUE TO BE LAUNCHED THIS AUTUMN AND WHEN COM-
PLETED WILL TAKE UP SERVICE ON THE AUSTRALIA AND PACIFIC RUN IN
CONJUNCTION WITH THE P & O LINER "CANBERRA", ALSO OF 40,000 TONS,
WHICH IS TO BE LAUNCHED A FEW MONTHS AFTER THE "ORIANA".
IT HAS BEEN CLAIMED THAT THERE IS MORE ALUMINIUM BEING USED IN
CONSTRUCTION OF THE ORIANA THAN WAS USED IN THE PRIDE OF AMERICA'S
SHIPPING WORLD, FLAG-SHIP OF THE UNITED STATES LINE, THE C
53,000 TONNER, "UNITED STATES". THE REASON FOR THIS IS THAT PRE-
VIOUSLY WHERE ALUMINIUM HAS BEEN USED TO ANY GREAT DEGREE, STEEL
STIFFENERS HAVE BEEN ESSENTIAL TO HELP WITH THE INTEGRAL RIGIDITY
REQUIRED IN THE CONSTRUCTION OF A LARGE SHIP OF PRESENT-DAY STAN-
DARDS.
THE ALUMINIUM SUPERSTRUCTURE WEIGHING JUST OVER 1,000 TONS, COM-
PRISES FIVE DECKS, TWO BRIDGE DECKS, AND ALL UPPER WORKS. THE
TOTAL AREA OF BULKHEAD AND DECK PLATING OF THIS MATERIAL IS ALMOST
350,000 SQ FT.
ABOUT 90% OF THE SUPERSTRUCTURE [struck through text] HAS BEEN ASSEMBLE
IN A PREFABRICATED FORM IN SHOPS ENTIRELY INDEPENDENT OF THE MAIN
YARDS.
THE COST OF THIS GIANT NEW SHIP, THE LARGEST PASSENGER VESSEL TO
BE CONSTRUCTED IN THIS COUNTRY SINCE THE ALL-TIME RECORD BREAKER,
"QUEEN ELIZABETH", 83,673 TONS, IS £12 1/2 M.
A MOST INTERESTING FEATURE OF THIS BEAUTIFUL NEW SHIP IS THE BULBOUS
FOREFOOT, THIS, IT APPEARS, ENABLES THE SHIP TO TRAVEL AT A VERY
MUCH HIGHER SPEED WITHOUT THE ADDED EXPENSE OF EXTRA POWER. A
FEATURE WHICH WILL NO DOUBT BE INCORPORATED IN MANY FUTURE BRITISH
SHIPS.
THIS PICTURE, TAKEN RECENTLY IN THE YARDS OF VICKERS ARMSTRONG,
SHOWS

A VIEW FROM THE STERN OF THE ORIANA SHOWING PLAINLY THE ALUMINIUM
SUPERSTRUCTURE BEGINNING TO RISE FROM THE STEEL HULL.

te.text:
FIRST PUBLICATION TUESDAY'S EVENINGS 7.1.47.

SWITCH OFF - OR THE GOVERNMENT WILL !

Very topical, in view of Mr Shinwell's stern warning
to the public over the week-end, are these photographs of
Fulham Power Station, largest electricity generating plant
in London and the largest municipal undertaking of its kind
in the whole country.

It produces 6 1/2 million units per day from five 60,000
K/W turbo-generators, and consumes between 2,500 and 3,000
tons of coal per day.

Incidentally, the photographs show how and what is meant
by "shedding the load", a technical term first given promin-
ence by the Fuel Minister.     The picture shows:

The frequency meter which indicates periodicity of
loading conditions. The danger point at which load must
be shed is shown in the picture.

DAILY HERALD

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION THURSDAY'S EVENINGS, July 24th.,

SILK WORMS THAT HELP BRITAIN'S EXPORTS
24.7.47.
A small but very important aid to British export trade is
being given by about six million silk worms which are being
reared at Lullingstone Castle Silk Farm, run by ZOE, LADY
HART DYKE, near Eynsford, Kent. The aim and object of the
farm, which is now getting going again after the war, is to
develop and assist production of raw silk in this country, the
Dominions, and the Colonies, and what started off as a girl's
hobby, developed on a business footing in 1932, is now a
flourishing industry housed in one of Britain's ancient homes.
The Lullingstone silkworms are known all over the world for
millions of them have been exported, and it was from their silk
that the Coronation Robes for the Queen and the Princesses
were made. One of the difficulties at present being ex-
perienced is the lack of mulberry leaves on which to feed
the worms, for the eighteen acre plantation at Lullingstone
is only producing about half the number of leaves required
to feed six million tiny mouths.
It is interesting to note that the method of using the silk
cocoon for spinning and weaving was first known in China at
least 3,000 years B.C. It was James I who endeavoured to
encourage silk worm rearing in this country by ordering the
importation and planting of thousands of mulberry trees, but
the Royal scheme was a failure. George I then took a keen
interest in the silk industry and in 1718 he granted a
patent to a certain John Appleton for silkworm rearing.
The picture shows a gleaming skein of raw silk being
tested layer by layer for any break s or flaws before it
is weighed and pressed for dispatching to the throwster and
weavers.

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

te.text: FILE - Indus - Fuel & Power, Electricity - Wind Power.

Lee
GIANT WINDMILL TO TEST POWER THEORY 29.6.53.
Going up today at Prae Wood, St. Albans, is a 100 kilo-
watt generator, part of a 100 ft tower which is to be
built with giant windmill blades on top to test
the efficiency of getting electric power in a big
scale from the wind. On the success of this experiment
will depend further efforts by the British Electricity
Authority to obtain power from the air.  The plan is
for two propeller blades of aluminium alloy to sweep a
circle 80ft in diameter on the tower. As the blades rotate
they will push out air by centrifugal force and form a
suction within the tower. The air drawn through the tower
would then work the generating turbines.   The work is
being done by Enfield Cables, Ltd.

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION THURSDAY'S DAILIES 3.3.60

BELFAST TO LAUNCH 150,000 TONS OF SHIPPING
3.3.60
FOR THE SECOND YEAR RUNNING, HARLAND AND WOLF LTD., OF 
BELFAST, ONE OF THE LARGEST SHIP-BUILDING COMPANIES IN THE
BRITISH ISLES, ARE LIKELY TO HEAD THE UOTPUT OF INDIVIDUAL
YARDS. LAST YEAR THEIR TOTAL GROSS TONNAGE PRODUCED WAS
124,211 TONS, WHILE IN THE FIRST SIX MONTHS OF THIS YEAR
THEY PLAN TO LAUNCH ALMOST 150,000 TONS. OF THE SIX SHIPS
TO BE LAUNCHED DURING THIS PERIOD, THE GIANT P. AND O.
LINER          CANBERRA" WILL BE ONE OF THE LARGEST,
TOTALLING 45,000 TONS. THE "CANBERRA", TO BE LAUNCHED ON
MARCH 16 BY DAME      PATTY MENZIES, WIFE OF THE
AUSTRALIAN PRIME MINISTER, IS THE LARGEST TO BE BUILT IN
BELFAST SINCE THE FIRST WORLD WAR, AND THE LARGEST SHIP TO
BE LAID DOWN IN ANY BRITISH YARD SINCE THE QUEEN ELIZABETH.
THE OTHER SHIPS TO BE LAUNCHED DURING THIS PERIOD ARE
TWO TANKERS, EACH 46,000 TONS, THE ROYAL MAIN LINE'S
"ARLANZA", 20,000 TONS, A CARGO SHIP OF 11,000 TONS,
AND A BULK CARRIER OF 12,000 TONS.

THE 45,000 TON LINER "CANBERRA" (LEFT) ANDTHE 20,000 TON
PASSENGER LINER "ARLANZA" MAKE AN IMPRESSIVE BACKGROUND
FOR PART OF ONE OF THE PROPELLOR SHAFTS DESTINED FOR THE
"CANBERRA".

te.text:
A RARE SIGHT IN THIS MODERN AGE. MJH/H.3.

In this modern age, the once familiar sight of the
village blacksmith, is now becoming very rare as
machinery replaces horses on the farm. In some
districts, however, where hilly land makes machinery
unpracticable, horses are still in use and the smith
is still very necessary. One such area is the Lake District
where blacksmiths can still be seen at work in their
old stone forges.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: A scene which is now becoming rare
is this one of horses waiting to be shod outside
the roadside blacksmith's forge at Crosthwaite, near
Windermere, Westmorland.

te.text:
E.M./HT.

THATCHING MACHINE HELPS ON THE FARM.

A machine invented and patented nearly half-a-century ago,
but never used, is now helping to solve labour problems on
British farms. It makes thatches for ricks at half the
cost and in a fifth of the time of the old hand method.
The matting can be made at any time by this machine and
can be stored in rolls till harvest time, so that ricks
can be immediately thatched to cut out risk of damage by
weather. These pictures, taken in Surrey, show the new
thatching machine in use.

Photo shows:- Miss Eleen Laxton, who was a dressmaker
before joining the Land Army, finds the work of stitching
thatch mats a familiar job.
FOX. 24th August, 1942. 279775.
[X mark across the Manchester rubber stamp]

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION THURSDAY'S EVENS, 3.6.48.

VITAL TO THE SUCCESS OF THE AFRICAN GROUNDNUT SCHEME.
Mac 3.6.48.
The movement of the groundnuts crop in Nigeria is
being held up through lack of sufficient rolling stock.
About half the 1947/8 crop of 250,000 tons up country
will still be awaiting transport when the new crop begins
to move in the Autumn. The urgency of the new locos to
replace those worn out ones now operating is vital ; all
haste is being made in production at the Vulcan Foundry
at Newton-le-Willows (Lancs) and additionally to the 20
already sent, another 42 are expected to go during the
year. The picture shows
a completed loco undergoing the final test in steam on
a set of rollers to try out the bearings and check valves.
They are of about 70 tons, with a guage of 3ft. 6ins.

COPYRIGHT PHOTO ISSUED BY
CENTRAL PRESS PHOTOS LTD.
INCORPORATING
Central News Illustrations Service,
119, FLEET STREET LONDON, E.C.4

te.text:
CRAFT "IN CHARACTER".                          MJH/HT.

"When the famous Cathedral Weaving Centre of Canterbury recently
took over an old building in Best Lane (Canterbury) as an
extension to their teaching facilities, they did not know
just how appropriate it was.  However, during alterations
the casing round the main chimney of the building was removed
and workmen discovered parts of centuries old looms and spinning
wheels.  This, combined with the strength of the first storey
floors proved that it had once been a weaving establishment
and it has been ascertained that this building is the place
where the Huguenot and Walloon weavers of the Middle Ages carried
on their art of weaving when they fled from the Continent, so the
present-day weavers have the right atmosphere for their craft.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS:  In the old Huguenot Centre, which has been
taken over by the Canterbury Weaving Centre, two young [illegible] girls
are seen working in the exact spot where the Huguenot and
Walloon weavers worked centuries ago.  On the left MISS MARGARET
WELLS of Faversham (Kent) is carding, whilst MISS DORIS BAILEY
sits at the spinning wheel on the original platform beneath
the eaves of the roof.

te.text:
HELPING THE RE-ARMAMENT PROGRAMME.                                  CH/AT

At a wharf near Greenwich two brothers, Charles and Alfred 
Robinson, are helping on the re-armament programme. They are 
probably the biggest of London's scrap metal merchants. Most 
of the scrap comes to them in pony carts and consists of 
dilapidated iron bedsteads, old perambulators, etc, collected 
by the smaller dealers. An interesting point is the absence 
of a magnetic crane to raise loads to waiting ships. They 
are too close to Greenwich Observatory and not allowed to 
have one.

Photo shows-  Loading a boat with scrap iron for South Wales 
for making armaments.
Fox May 18th. 37.

te.text:
THE SHAPE OF THINGS TO COME. MJH/RS. 
Hugh Pope, one of the assistant architects working on the 
new Coventry Cathedral, has built himself an experimental 
studio in the grounds of his home on Kingston Hill (Surrey), 
made entirely of glass with a light timber frame. The interior 
is lined with panels which can be taken out or put in, to 
suit the weather and lighting wanted. The actual frame of 
150 separate triangles was put up by Mr. Pope, his wife Jennie 
and a friends, artist Peter Kermode, over a weekend "Though I 
confess", he adds, "that the foundations and glazing were done 
by a building firm to my design. I believe that there will 
be many houses and religious buildings constructed in this way 
in the future". (THIS CAPTION MUST NOT BE ALTERED). 

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: MRS. JENNIE POPE, seen taking a vase 
of flowers into the glass studio, which her husband has 
built in the grounds of their home at Kingston Hill (Surrey).

activity: an underwater search for oil in Gambia involving a waterborne seismic survey and a depth-charge like explosion

te.text:
FRIDAY'S
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION THURSDAY'S DAILIES, March 19th.

AN UNDERWATER SEARCH FOR OIL IN GAMBIA
                                      9.3.56.
The British Petroleum Company's prospecting subsidiary,
D'Arcy Exploration Company, is now searching for oil in
Gambia, the British Colony and Protectorate on the West
coast of Africa. As a first step, a waterborne seismic
survey or more than 200 miles of the River Gambia has
begun. This is being conducted from the "SONIC", a
former landing craft, which has carried out similar work
in the Persian Gulf. The seismic survey will provide useful
information not only on the rock structure beneath the
river bed, but also on that below the neighbouring land.
It is a quicker method of making a preliminary survey than
a similar operation on land, since dense forests fringe
the River Gambia. Seismic surveys ascertain the shape of
subterranean rock structures by recording on delicate
instruments, the vibrations set up by explosive charges
fired either underground or under water.
      The picture shows a "depth-charge" like explosion
in the seaward approaches of the river Gambia after a
charge had been dropped overboard from the "Sonic".

te.text:
GLOUCESTERSHIRE. 
 
 W9/4 
 
 HARVESTING IN MAY. 
 
 Rye Harvesting, peculiar to a few parts of Gloucestershire is now 
 in full swing. Unlike the corn harbest the crop is not dried but 
 cut anf given to the cattle green as a spring food, as required. 
 This means an economy to the farmer as he is thus able to keep his 
 cattle off the young grass thereby ensuring a full hay crop in a 
 short time. 
 
 Photo shows - An armful of freshly cut rye at Coalpit Heath, near 
 Bristol, Glos. The seed is sown in August and harvested in May. 
 
 FOX. MAY 10th. 35.

as Causes Ex-M.P.

A most important feature of all Britain's exports is
the fact that the many and variable types of machinery
necessayy to create these exports, is dependent upon
ball-bearings. The types of these bearings range from
the most minute to those in the giant class, and there

where millions of bearings are produced annually. Though
not always directly concerned in exporting, bearings are
to be found in a wide range of exported commodities such
as cars, machinery, railway-rolling stock, ect. The

activity: Harvesting wheat by night using a combine harvester fitted with headlights.

te.text:
NIGHT HARVEST.                             MJH/MAE.

Farmers all over the country have, this year, experienced
great difficulty in completing their harvesting programme,
due to the frequent wet weather. They have been forced to
do their harvesting an hour or two at a time, whenever the
weather permitted. One Gloucestershire farmer, Major
J. Bradish-Ellanes of Haymes Farm, Cleeve Hill decided to
make the most of a recent fine day by continuing with his
harvesting by night until it was finished. This was
accomplished by the use of a Combine fitted with headlights.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: Harvesting wheat by night on Major J.
Bradish-Ellanes', Haymes Farm, Cleeve Hill (Glos), with the
aid of a Combine fitted with headlights. By this method, the
harvest was completed shortly before mid-night, the wheat
remaining dry after a warm sunny day.

DRILLING THE SEA-BED FOR OIL OFF THE DORSET COAST.

   The first offshore oil well to be drilled in the coastal
waters of Great Britain, has commenced operation on the
Lulworth Banks about 2 1/2 miles offshore from Lulworth Cove,

barge weighing 650 tons which has four retractable legs
which rest on the seabed.   From the 87 foot mast mounted

activity: A depth charge is fired about 200 yards astern of the survey vessel 'Texin' during North Sea geophysical operations to aid selection of drilling locations for oil and gas.

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION IN DAILIES
OF FRIDAY 9TH OCTOBER 1964

NORTH SEA GEOPHYSICAL OPERATIONS.
ERF.	G.	OCTOBER 1964
BRITISH PETROLEUM HAS BEEN AWARDED PRODUCTION
LICENCES BY THE MINISTER OF POWER, COVERING
SOME 2,200 SQUARE MILES IN AREA TO SEARCH FOR
AND PRODUCE OIL AND NATURAL GAS UNDER THE
NORTH SEA ADJACENT TO THE UNITED KINGDOM. THE
AREAS LIE OFF THE COAST OF DURHAM, YORKSHIRE
AND LINCOLNSHIRE.
			THE COMPANY HAS DRAWN UP PLANS FOR
ITS OWN SUBSTANTIAL DRILLING PROGRAMME. THE B.P.
AREA HAS BEEN DIVIDED INTO THREE PRODUCTION LICENCES, IN
EACH OF WHICH ONE DEEP TEST WILL INITIALLY BE
DRILLED: THE PROGRAMME FOR FURTHER TEST DRILLING
WILL BE ABOUT 12,000 FEET IN DEPTH AND WILL COST
AT LEAST £500,000. DRILLING OPERATIONS WILL
COMMENCE AS EARLY AS PRACTICABLE IN 1965.
GEOPHYSICAL WORK HAS ALREADY BEGUN IN ORDER
TO AID SELECTION OF DRILLING LOCATIONS.
PHOTO SHOWS:

A DEPTH CHARGE IS FIRED ABOUT 200 YARDS ASTERN
OF THE SURVEY VESSEL "TEXIN". THESE CHARGES
WHICH ARE PRIMED IN A SPECIAL CAGE, ATTACHED
TO THE FIRING LINE AND JETTISONED INTO WATER,
ARE FIRED AT THE RATE OF ALMOST ONE A MINUTE
DURING DAYLIGHT HOURS. THE EFFECT OF THE SHOCK
WAVES FROM THE DEPTH CHARGES ECHOED FROM THE
ROCK FORMATION BELOW THE SEA BED, ARE RELAYED
BY THE "STREAMER". SIGNALS FROM THE SHOCK WAVE
ARE FED INTO THE SHIP VIA THE "STREAMER" AND RECORDED
ON TAPE AS WELL AS BEING PHOTOGRAPHICALLY REPRODUCED
AS AN IMMEDIATE 	VISUAL CHECK.

G. 10055

SUN
PROPERTY
9 OCT 1964
Please return to
ART Library

te.text:
BUILDING SHIPS FOR THE MERCHANT NAVY.  E.M./MCN.

British shipyards are launching merchant vessels with
all possible speed; a 10,000 tonner now gets its last
coat of paint only 5 1/2 months after the keel-laying.
Widespread use of prefabrication has helped this speed-
up and welding instead of rivetting has saved time and
steel. This series of pictures taken at a shipyard
shows ships in various stages of completion in the stocks.
At the present rate of progress it will not be long
before these same ships are on active service for Britain.

Photo shows:- A view of the shipyard showing two
ships in stocks.

"HIGH TIME" FOR HOP STRINGING.        MJH/rs.

In the hop fields of Kent, work is now in progress on the
annual task of "hop-stringing" - that is fixing up the
criss-cross strings from the top of the poles, along which
the growing hop-bines will be trained. To do this work,
then men have to perform a "circus act" - for the only way
then can rig up the strings and fix hooks to them, is by
walking on stilts.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS:  42-years-old MR. GEORGE WELLS seen
"stil walking" in the Whitbread hop-field at Beltring, Paddock
Wood (Kent) where "stringing" is now in progress. Mr. Wells
has been doing this work every year for the past 20 years.
Beneath him pushing the barrow of twine is Mr. BERT BISHOP (54).

STUDENTS CLAIM URANIUM FIND IN CORNISH TIN MINE   D/P.1.

Six students, members of the Scientific and Geological
Society of Worksop College, Notts., claim to have found
a rich seam of uranium in the old Wheal Edward tin mine
near St. Just, Cornwall. The students are spending a
month's holidays volunteer workers for Mr. Paul Stein
of London who owns the rights of the mine. They have dug
out 18 cwts of rough ore, which they claim is 25% uranium
oxide. It has been sent to London for examination by the
Ministry of Supply.

PHOTO SHOWS: Mr. W. Billing, a skilled miner of St. Just,
is seen in centre examining the uranium in a piece of ore,
surrounded by some of the student miners.

te.text:
BUYERS FROM REST OF WORLD FOR £1,000,000 WORTH OF FURS IN LONDON

There are now in London buyers from all parts of the world
attending the fur sales conducted by the London Fur Sales
Committee.  All through the winter valuable furs have been
collected by the distant posts in Northern Canada and have been
sent, mostly by slow and arduous travel, to London Most of
these posts are controlled by the Hudson Bay Company who own
most of the skins offered for sale in London.  About £1,000,000worth
are now at the Hudson Bay warehouse in Queen Victoria Street
and are being daily auctioned.

Photo shows:-  Buyers, wearing overalls to protect their clothes,
examining white fox skins before bidding at the Hudson Bay
sale today.
FOX Jany 26th.

activity: blacksmith ROBERT MARTIN seen at work outside his old stone forge at Ardigon, Killyleagh, showing horses and mending cart wheels

te.text:
AN EMERALD ISLE SMITHY.  MJH/M. 8.

A charming characteristic scene, fast disappearing from
the landscape of the British Isles in this mechanised age,
is the sight of the village smithy at work outside his
forge. However, in a few districts, particularly where
the contours of the land are hilly, making machines
impracticable, so that the horse is still a very necessary
part of farm life, there is still plenty of work for
the blacksmith. One such place is at Ardigon, Killyleagh,
Co. Down (N. Ireland), where the 'smith, 78-years-old
Robert Martin [strike-through] still gets enough of the work he loves
to keep him busy. Mr. Martin, a typical bit of "Ould 
Oirland" has been a blacksmith for 64 years.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: 78-years-old blacksmith ROBERT MARTIN,
seen at work outside his old stone forge at Ardigon, Killyleagh,
Co. Down, N. Ireland, where he can still find plenty of work,
showing horses, mending cart wheels etc.
FOX PHOTOS JUNE 16TH. 1955.

activity: Bus conductresses (clippies) demonstrating outside the Transport and General Workers' Union headquarters in Gower Street for equal rights, while a union official lectures their leader Kathleen Fincham.

te.text:
THE setting is the pavement
outside the London headquarters
of the Transport and General
Workers' Union in Gower Street.
Inside a meeting of busmen had
broken up after conductresses
marched in carrying banners
saying, 'We refuse to be
second-class workers.' The
women want to be allowed to drive
buses, and claim improved
pensions and sick pay. Rather
than discuss their grievances, the
men adjourned their meeting to
the scorn of the women who said,
'What are you afraid of?' This is
nothing but bigotry.' The words
must have smarted the busmen,
one of whom was George Fincham,
husband of the clippies' leader,
Kathy Fincham. Outside, Mr. and
Mrs. Fincham held a little meeting
of their own, and were joined by
another clippie, Doris Scott. Then
a union official arrived and gave
Mrs. Fincham a lecture on how not
to conduct union business. This
is the tableau in the picture, with
the official (in cap) lecturing Mrs.
Fincham, while her husband and
Doris Scott look on. Later Mrs.
Fincham went home to cook her
husband's dinner, at which the
debate continued.

JONES. SUN. 10.12.68.
Bus Conductresses Demonstrate at monthly conference T.G.W.U.
XXXXXX Women Clippies demonstrated outside the Headquarters of the T.G.W.U.
Gower St, nr Euston., before gate-crashing the conference with only men
in attendance. Immediately they entered the men decided to adjourn. Mrs
Kathleen Fincham, spokesman for the clippies who comes from Winchmore Hill,
had her husband George, a Union worker, driver in the meeting. After the
walk out by the men, Mrs Fincham was joined her husband George, seen bareheaded
on right, and another clippie Doris Scott on extreme right, xxxxx when
Mrs Fincham, seen holding bag, was called apart by a Union member and given
a talking to.
INDUS...MISC. WORKERS WOMEN EQUAL PAY ETC

activity: A general view of Mosley Common Colliery in Boothstown, Lancashire, showing a modern pithead as part of a reconstruction scheme.

te.text:
LANCASHIRE'S LARGEST COLLIERY
UNDER RECONSTRUCTION

The completion of half the coal
preparation plant, marks the end of the
first stage of the reconstruction scheme at
MOSLEY COMMON COLLIERY , BOOTHSTOWN, (Lancs.)
The largest colliery in Lancashire, Mosley
Common, employs more than 2,700 workers. When
the new scheme is complete coal from Sandhole
and Newtown collieries, in addition to that of
Mosley Common, will be wound electrically up
the one new shaft-now being completed.
Ultimately , 8,000 tons of coal each day will
be brought up this shaft from the three
collieries in two shifts. When finally complete
the MOSLEY COMMON coal preparation plant will
be the largest of its kind in Great Britain.
It is designed to treat a minimum of 600
tons of coal an hour, or working two shifts
8,000 tons per day- the whole of the coal as mined
with no hand selection whatever.
Large pieces of coal will be broken mechanically
to a maximum size of eight inches ( a provision
which domestic users will appreciate) and even the
very finest sizes of dust will be cleaned to a
low ash content. Washed slack or "smalls" will
be dried by a centrifugal machine at high speed
- thus enabling direct despatch from the pit
instead of having to stand insidings drying
for upwards of 24 hours. The total cost will be
more than half a million pounds.

PHOTO SHOWS:- A general view of MOSLEY COMMON
COLLIERY, BOOTHSTOWN, Lancashire , showing a modern
pithead

FOX PHOTOS Feb 1950

PROPERTY OF THE

te.text:
A TYPICALLY ENGLISH CRAFT. PC/VAN.

One of the most typically English crafts
must surely be the making of cricket bats
and at Benjamin Warsop & Sons Limited, St.
John's Wood, London, near the famous Lord's
ground, fine bats have been produced for many
years. Some of the orders are bulk, for
large sports stores and export, but, some are
specially tailored to suit the requirements
of the top batsmen throughout the world.
Special orders are often produced under the
watchful eyes of 87 year-old, Mr.George Edward Hunt,
who started learning his craft at the age of
twenty-one - he is now the managing director
of the company but can nearly always be
found in one of the workshops supervising
the construction of the fine cricket bats.

Photo shows. DAVID MARKHAM, of Watford, Herts., a
young craftsman, seen fixing a handle to a new
cricket bat.

te.text:
Ind - Engineering - Machinery etc.                CAPTION

KEARNEY & TRECKER-C.V.A. LAUNCHES FIRST
BRITISH-BUILT MILWAUKEE-MATIC
---------------------------------------

The first British-built Milwaukee-Matic machining centre
has been introduced by Kearney & Trecker-C.V.A. Ltd.,
the south coast machine tool enterprise. It is the
Series Ea model which will carry out the individual
operations of milling, drilling, boring, reaming and
tapping from one point without the need to transfer the
workpiece to another machine. The entire operation is
carried out by punched tape control from a computer and
provides dramatic savings in production and setup time
compared to conventional methods. A feature of the Ea
is its ability to meet any machining requirement from
the average small batch manufacture to long run product-
ion. With the Ea model tool changes are made auto-
matically in five seconds from a drum-type tool magazine
which holds 15 tools.

activity: Hostess Elizabeth Sterland with Swedish businessman Alv Gregersen at the Royal Garden Hotel in London.

te.text:
TWO ATTRACTIVE girls,
eager to be of assistance,
waited at London Airport
yesterday to welcome
visitors from all over
Europe attending a con-
ference here.
But they waited in vain.
For their stall was so well
concealed that only one
delegate out of 950 man-
aged to find it.
And last night the firm
which organised the con-
ference of Pulp and Paper
Industrial Technology did
not trouble to conceal
their anger.
Mrs. Fay Pannell, who
introduced the hostess
service for delegates, said:
"London Airport have not
been at all helpful. They
are, in fact, very difficult
to get on with.
'Useless'
"If the airport already
had an efficient reception
system, other people would
not be needed to do it."
Mrs. Pannell's com-
plaint: "We felt the girls
should be in a good posi-
tion in the airport lounge.
But we have been given
a small stall right at the
end of the main concourse

-and charged £55 rent
for three days.
"It is useless - just
money down the drain."
Still, there was no lack
of attention for the dele-
gates last night at the
Royal Garden Hotel, head-
quarters of the con-
ference.
Fifteen hostesses - each
paid £3 a day - were on
duty in their couturier-
designed uniforms. All in-
tent on maintaining what
Mrs. Pannell called "a
strictly business relation-
ship with the delegates."

CHRIS BARHAM  SUN  4.9.66
CONFERENCE HOSTESSES.  STORY BARRY FRASER.
An organisation called Conference Services provides hostesses to help
business men at London conferences.
O.P.S. Hostess Elizabeth Sterland (20) with some colleagues and Swedish
businessman Alv Gregersen at London's Royal Garden Hotel today.

NORTHANTS.
BRITAIN LAYS ITS FIRST TELEVISION CABLE.

Post Office enginers have begun to lay the first longe
distance television cable in Britain. The cable will stretch
from London to Birmingham. There is only one wire in the
cable. The wire will be able to carry 20 voices
simultaneously , will relay sound, broadcast and television
programmes . As it is hoped that a regular B.B.C. public
television service will begin next June it is possible
that the B.B.C. may televise the Coronation ceremony.

Photo shows- Laying miles of television cable at
Northampton to-day, the first television cable in Britain.
Fox Feb 20th. 36.

activity: Princess Elizabeth representing the King at the Trooping the Colour Parade, photographed at the saluting base in front of Buckingham Palace with members of the Royal Family on the balcony.

te.text:
PRINCESS ELIZABETH REPRESENTS THE KING AT TROOPING  7-6-51
THE COLOUR

H.M. the King was represented by Princess Elizabeth 
at today's King Birthday Trooping the Colours Parade
at the Horse Guards Parade.  The Princess, riding her
chestnut, Winston, wore the scarlet tunic of colonel 
of the Grenadier Guards with a dark blue riding skirt.
Her tricorne hat with white plume fixed into a grenade
on the left side is an exact copy of that of a colonel 
of the Regiment of 1745. 

INP PHOTO SHOWS: Princess Elizabeth photographed at the 
saluting base as the Guards march past 
in front of Buckingham Palace. On the 
balcony watching can be seen, the Queen, 
Queen Mary, Prince Charles, Princess 
Margaret and King Haakon and Princess 
Astrid of Norway. 

PICTURE BY E. WING
P/268, Com/53498  INTERNATIONAL NEWS PHOTOS

72, FLEET STREET, LONDON, E.C.4
TEL. CENTRAL 5644

PROPERTY OF 
DAILY HERALD
RCD. - 8 JUN 1951
PLEASE RETURN 
TO

te.text: File INDUS Aviation Post War - Air Liners Brit - Bristol "Brabazon"

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION MONDAY, Oct 21st.
ENGLISH VILLAGE MAKES WAY FOR GIANT PLANE
20.10.46.
Sacrificed to the cause of progress, the village of CHARLTON,
near Bristol, England, has been demolished to make room for
a runway spacious enough to allow the first take-off of the
giant Bristol "Brabazon" air liner prototype now under con-
struction at the famous works. A vast assembly hall is
also being built because she cannot be put together in any
existing building.
Features of the great aircraft are - wing span 230ft, height
50ft at rudder, and length 177ft. All-up weight 125 tons,
and sleeping berths for 80 passengers for night travel. It is
designed to fly direct between London and New York or
Montreal, and gas turbines in the wings accessible during
flight will give her a speed of 350 mph at 35,000 ft and her
range will be 5,000 miles. The picture shows workmen fixing
centre section wing ribs with the giant fuselage taking shape
in the background. The man in the wing illustrates how it
is possible to attend to the power units, which are built into
the wing, in flight.

activity: the bathroom of a dilapidated house under investigation for the Rachman housing scandal

te.text:
PETER RACHMAN is dead, but fear
still haunts St. Stephen's Gardens
and Chepstow Road, Paddington—heart
of the empire where once he squeezed
rents from crumbling bricks.
Landlords, some of them linked with Rachman,
are selling properties as fast as they can. New
landlords are taking over with the aim of making
a fast profit. They want the tenants out, either
to resell at a profit or
else to pack in more
people paying more
money.
And so the rent bullies
still bluster at the door in
Rachman's streets.
Mrs. Annie O'Keefe has
found that a change of land-
lord does not necessarily
mean an improvement on
the Rachman regime.
She has a single top-floor room
at 11, St. Stephen's Gardens.
Her tenancy is protected under
the Rent Act.
But in May the property
changed hands and Mrs. O'Keefe
now pays her rent to the Dis-
tinctive Property Company, who
have an address at 110, Shore-
ditch High Street, London.
STRUCK HER
Since they took over Mrs.
O'Keefe has been subjected to
continual threats, designed, she
believes, to make her quit the
property.
Twice she has been called on
by a man called Richards and
another named De Freitas (a
former associate of Rahman).
They claimed to be acting for
the landlord.
Richards and de Freitas
demanded the rent — which
was not due for several days.
Mrs. O'Keefe keeps the door
of her room chained. On the
second visit, however, the two
men forced the door. In doing
so they bruised Mrs. O'Keefe's
knee. She has also told her
solicitor that one of them struck
her on the arm.
The pair went away when
Mrs. O'Keefe threatened to get
the police. And since she put
the matter in the hands of a
solicitor she has not been visited
again.

DAILY HERALD
Copyright
Photograph
BY L. BLANDFORD
NUMBER..................

This is the bathroom at 13, St. Stephen's Gardens, one of
the houses visited by the Herald investigating team

BLANDFORD.D.H. 18.7.63. Story R. Adams.
RACHMAN STORY.
O.P.S. The Bathroom in No. 13 St. Stephens Gardens, Paddington.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
18 JUL 1963
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

activity: Operating a digging machine in the construction of the London Airport traffic tunnel.

te.text:
LONDON AIRPORT TRAFFIC TUNNEL GROWS  D/FM

Considerable progress has been made during the
summer months on the 4-way vehicular traffic
tunnel which will link London Airport terminal
area with the ondon-Bath road. When completed
this tunnel will be the only means of communi-
cation between the airport and the surrounding
land area and will be approached by two long
ramps leading from the Bath road, one of which is
almost surfaced. The central area will house all
the passenger and administrative buildings, which
are at present strung out along the northern
perimeter of the Airport, and will be dominated
by a lofty Control Tower. The 2,600 ft. long
tunnel comprises two single-way traffic roadways
flanked on either side by two single-way passenger
and cycle ways.

PHOTO SHOWS: Operating a digging machine in the
construction of the London Airport traffic
tunnel.

COAL BOARD HAS ITS OWN UNIFORM.

With the handing over of the mines
to public ownership, a new uniform
has appeared at Lansdowne House,
Berkeley Square, W., temporary
headquarters of the National Coal Board.
The uniform, which resembles a
police inspector's, is dark blue with
patch pockets and chromium buttons.
The initials 'NCB' are on the lapels.
Members of the staff who have to wear
the uniform are still uncertain about
whether they will have to give up
clothing coupons for it.
PHOTO SHOWS:- Mr. Albert B. Turton,
chief porter at Lansdowne House, wearing
the new uniform. 'I like it', he says,
'but the coupons...?'
CHI January 1st 1947 PN.r.

activity: building construction using hot concrete to allow work to continue in freezing temperatures at a site in Houndsditch, London

te.text: Industry.. Building and Construction.. Misc... Anti bad weather measures

HOT CONCRETE BEATS THE WINTER

Britain's building industry can now beat
frost and snow - with hot concrete. Work
goes on at this large building site in
Houndsditch, London, even when the temperature
drops well below zero. Tons of aggregate and
hundreds of gallons of water are heated by
Calor propane before being fed into the mixer.
As a result, the concrete sets before frost
can attack it. The process was developed by
the Calor Gas company earlier this year.

Contractors at the Houndsditch site are
Myton Ltd., who are erecting an eight-floor
block of offices and shops, and a 14-storey
car park for City and Southern Properties Ltd.
Architects for the project are R. Seifert and
Partners; consulting engineers, C. J. Pell and
Partners; quantity surveyors, John Reddick
and Partners.

Further enquiries: David Harrison,
Frank O'Shanohun Associates
Ltd.,
34 Bouverie Street,
London, E.C.4.

FLEet Street 9891

NO REPRODUCTION FEE.

te.text:
NEW LEASE OF LIFE FOR OLD COTTAGE.     MJH/MAE.
An old Cotswold stone cottage at Winson in the Coln
Valley (Glos), belonging to Col. R. Henriques, is now
in the process of repair and modernisation, one of many
such restoration schemes which are now taking place in
the Cotswolds. Many of the picturesque Cotswold villages
are being greatly improved by such work, undertaken on the
incentive given by the Slum Clearance Act and Council
Grants to owners to repair old cottages in their original
style, but with all modern interior conveniences.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: MR. H.W. DAY (left) a local builder
whose family have specialised in Cotswold stone work and
roofing for generations seen selecting stones for the
work on the cottage at Winson (Glos). He has restored nearly
20 such cottages in the Coln Valley. With him (right) MR.
M. DAY, stone roof tiler, is seen cutting roofing tiles.
