te.text: HOME + HOUSING - PREWAR ONLY - HOUSING MISC - DEMOS - STEPNEY '39

RENT STRIKERS SPEND WHITSUN PREPARING SECOND 
 LINE OF DEFENCE.      28.5.39.

 MOST OF THE 380 TENANTS OF LANGDALE MANSIONS AND BRADY 
 STREET MANSIONS, STEPNEY, ARE SPENDING THEIR WHITSUN 
 STRENGTHENING THE DEFENCES WHICH THEY HAVE ERECTED AT 
 THE FLATS. EVER SINCE THE TENANTS WERE THREATENED WITH 
 EVICTION THE TWO BLOCKS OF FLATS HAVE BEEN IN A STATE OF 
 SIEGE. SIDE PASSAGES LEADING TO ADJOINING PROPERTIES 
 HAVE BEEN LOOSED BY WOODEN BARRIERS AND WIRES AND THIS 
 WEEKEND A SECOND LINE OF BARRIERS IS BEING BUILT. PICKETS 
 ARE ON DUTY DAY AND NIGHT AND TOP FLOOR TENANTS HAVE BEEN 
 SUPPLIED WITH SOOT AND FLOUR. IF FURTHER SUMMONSES ARRIVE 
 THE TENANTS WILL ACCEPT THEM THROUGH THE BARS, BUT NOT 
 PROCESS-SERVER OR BAILIFF WILL BE ADMITTED.

 O.P.S. A PICKED ON DUTY AT ONE OF THE BARRICADED GATES, 
 EXAMINES A TENANT'S PASS BEFORE ADMITTING HER THIS 
 MORNING. EVERYBODY BUT HAVE PASSES TO ENTER OR 
 LEAVE THE FLATS. 541/B. KEYS ONE

a fast dying profession, for blacksmiths are now
becoming a rarity.
Motor Engineer is the new term for where Nat used
to shoe over 200 horses six times a year, now only
20 come to him to be reshod.
Nat's father was a blacksmith as were four of his
eight brothers of whom he is the only one left.
In spite of the lack of horses to shoe, Nat
persuaded his 40 year old son to learn the craft
and now when Nat passes on, Ronald will become the
fourth generation of Barber - Blacksmith.
Nat boasts of the time he shoed famous racehorses
in the district.
Nat estimates that he has made and forged 25,000
shoes in his 53 years and hopes to make a few more
thousand yet. He works from dawn till dusk six
days a week throughout the year.
There is another son, Horace, profession motor
engineer.
O.P.S.1    70 year old Nat. Barber at the forge
           at Milford Mill.

SAYERS.        1983-5236/90001        18.10.38.

THEY WERE IN A "DEVILISH MOOD".
Imperial Airways overcome menace of mosquitoes
in tropical countries.

to their laboratories in Battersea, to see a
device similar to that now employed by many
London Hospitals for disinfecting their wards.
It consists of a portable vaporising machine
which permeates the atmosphere with a pyrethrum
insecticide which kills the mosquitoes which are
liable to carry disease within a few minutes.
O.P.S.
25 mosquitoes in each of these little cages
were nice and warm in front of a gas fire,
so that they would be right on form and in
fine fettle for the demonstration.  It is
needless to say none of them survived the test.

activity: The prepackaging installation at Charringtons depot at Radley where solid fuel is packed into multiwall paper sacks and palletised for storage.

te.text: Ind - Fuel - Coal Depots nd Dumps inc. Sale of

Prepacked solid fuel is being sold in Oxford from this week by Charrington
Gardner Locket delivered in 56 lb. and 28 lb. paper sacks. Known as
Pak-o-Fuel, the delivery service is so clean an operation that the prepacked
fuel is brought to the consumer by coalmen dressed in white overalls.
Picture shows:  The prepackaging installation at Charringtons depot at
Radley, near Oxford, where a wide range of solid fuel is packed into
56 lb. and 28 lb. multiwall paper sacks at high speed.
By using the latest method of palletisation, sufficient quantities of the
prepacked fuel are being stored to meet peak demands.  The empty pallets
(left foreground) are fed one by one onto a platform which is then raised
hydraulically to the level of the sack conveyor.
The operator has only to guide the sack into position on the pallet
without having to completely lift them.  The operator can rotate the
platform to load the pallet and lower it sufficiently to load the next
layer of sacks.
When the pallet is fully loaded it is lowered and moved sideways on to
the rails (right foreground), where it is removed by fork lift truck,
and the same movement pushes the next empty pallet into position on the
platform.

Issued on behalf of:
Reed Medway Sacks Limited,
Larkfield,
Kent.

Enquiries: Allen Loates
Reed House,
82 Piccadilly,
London. W.1.
GROsvenor 4020

50 to 100,000 FULLY BOUND BOOKS PER WEEK.
Some of the largest Perfector printing
machines in Europe: Printing 64 pages on
each side of the sheet.
The copy from the author goes to Linotype
machines - they have a keyboard similar to
that of a typewriter - which transforms the
printed word into metal type.  The type is
made up into a page form which has a
facsimile taken off it in paper flong,
from which the metal cast is produced.
Plates are assembled in special order on the
bed of the printing machine and after the
application of ink, the printed sheet is
produced.
The printed sheet goes through nearly half-
a dozen operations such as folding, gathering,
sewing and cutting, when it is transformed
into the bound copy sold to the public.
Real leather is used for the making of cases.
Real 22 carat gold is applied to the lettering.

Above is one of the machines used in the

the concave front, and the convex back and
hinge.

activity: Joey, a pit pony, coming up from Carl Colliery in Ashington for the last time upon his retirement.

te.text:
HAVE you ever wondered
what happens to pit
ponies when their life's
work underground is
done?
Last week, after seeing this
picture — it shows Joey,
the pony, coming up from
Carl Colliery, Ashington,
for the last time — I set
out to find the answer.
It shocked me. I was told that
1,000 pit ponies are "retired"
by the Coal Board every year,
and 700 of them are destroyed.
Simply because there are not
enough suitable homes for
them. Rather than condemn
ponies used to the comrade-
ship of the miners under-
ground to lonely lives in
empty fields, they are pain-
lessly put to sleep.
One man is trying desperately
hard to find a better way out.
Chief Inspector Bill Burr, of
the R.S.P.C.A. at Scarborough,
spends all his spare time find-
ing homes for retired pit
ponies.
Last year alone he rescued 50

ponies. He does it as much
for the miners as for the
ponies. "I've seen many a
miner cry when his pony has
gone up the shaft for the last
time," says Bill Burr.
But he agrees with the Coal
Board that empty fields are
no places for retired ponies.
They can only go to those who
have proper stabling.
No pony must be used com-
mercially for pleasure rides—
and horse dealers are strictly
barred.
"They work underground for at
least 10 years. They are
much loved by the men so
they deserve proper care in
their retirement," says the
Coal Board with an unex-
pected warmth of feeling.
Chief Inspector Burr should
get more help for his work of
mercy. Over 7,000 ponies toil
to give us coal. It's dear
enough, I agree. But not all
that dear, surely?
Industry - Fuel & Power - Coal - Pits - Ponies.

Under Carl
from Ashwell
heaven's a home.

te.text:
SMITH  D.H.  17.6.63.
BUILDING COLLAPSES ON WORKMEN NEAR LYCEUM.  Story P. Moorhead.
O.P.S.
Workmen and Firemen work frantically to release the 
trapped men.

THEY were pulling down a house in
Exeter Street, just off the Strand.
The usual rough hearty banter, the
usual soloist singing a pop tune, and all
the loud thud and crackle that goes with
demolition work.
Then it happened. Tons of brick and
plaster roared down.
SWEAT
And underneath is one of their mates.
With bare hands they sweat into the
job of freeing him, grabbing through the
dust and debris at the bricks and rafters.
Firemen arrive. Together they go on
heaving away the rubble, through
precious minute after precious minute.
Bleeding fingers torn on masonry are
ignored. So is the threatening danger
of another fall of overhanging brickwork.
Forty-five minutes are gone.
TEARS
A hand is spotted . . A workmate
shouts: "I've found him."
Ambulancemen move in. Workmates
and firemen on their knees scoop away
the dirt and wood and debris from the
buried man.
Shoulders droop. Men take off their
caps . .
They have lost their race against time.
Their mate is dead.

te.text:
224476  LUD
TAKE A CLOSE LOOK - THEY'RE GOLD.
London: Glittering, golden sovereigns, a small
fortune in gold coins, some of a number which
the Royal Mint in London is making so that craftsmen
can 'keep their hand in'.
The last time sovereigns were minted for issue was
in 1917. Some were struck in 1925, these bear that
date, and the head of George V on one side and the
traditional George and Dragon on the other.
The gold came from the Bank of England, as as
sovereigns, each weighing 123.27 grains, will go
back there.
The coins are worth far more than their face value
of one pound.

te.text:
V. 23046.

STEPNEY-POPLAR RECONSTRUCTION AREA.

    The London County Council will consider on Tuesday
next, 5th., February, initial proposals for the
long-term redevelopment of an extensive area of
1,960 acres in Stepney and Poplar.
    This photograph shows a model indicating the lines
of the proposed redevelopment by the Council of an
area of 33 1/2 acres at Ocean Street, Stepney (part
of the Stepney-Poplar Reconstruction Area), as a
new housing site. (See also photograph No. V. 23246).
    The development scheme provides for mixed types
of accommodation consisting of two-storey terrace
houses with gardens, and three-storey, four storey
and eight-storey blocks of flats. The total
accommodation will be 1,145 dwellings and in
addition 12 shops, 3 children's fitted playgrounds
and about 90 perambulator sheds will be provided.
Lifts will be provided in the eight-storey blocks of
flats and provision will be made for a nursery group
of from 30 to 40 children in one of the blocks
of dwellings, with a small playing space adjoining.
February 1946.

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION TUESDAY'S EVENINGS, Jan 21st.
"QUEEN ELIZABETH" OF THE AIR TAKES SHAPE
21.1.47.
In the early summer it is hoped that the Bristol "Brabazon"
prototype of Britain's largest airplane, will make her first
flight.
Work on the giant aircraft began just over a year ago, and
her construction will have involved an outlay of £4,000,000
the destruction of a village and a golf course, and the
building of a special runway costing £2,000,000.
She will be 177ft long with a wing span of 230ft (30ft longer
than the distance between the main structures of Tower
Bridge), and weight 130 tons, and eight Centaurus gas-turbines
of 2500 hp each will power her. "Brabazon's" later models
will carry 100 passengers in comfort at 250 mph on British
Atlantic services. In this picture two men are working high
up on one of the platforms built among the scaffolding which
surrounds the massive fuselage which nestled in a steel
cradle.

THIS IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

COPYRIGHT PHOTO ISSUED BY
CENTRAL PRESS PHOTOS LTD.
INCORPORATING

119, FLEET STREET LONDON.

MAKING YORKSHIRE'S BREAD POTS.                 C.

On Ogden Moors between Bradford and Halifax there still exists

are still made.  The old potters wheel, more than 200 years

produced at this pottery.

NO FREEZE-UP AT JACKBLOCK

normal working has continued on Costain's Jackblock site in

EX SERVICEMEN'S FAMILIES MOVE INTO EMPTY ARMY HUTS -
WAR OFFICE DECIDE TO TAKE NO ACTION.

Unable to find homes elsewhere because of the housing shortage,
ex Servicemen and their wives and children have moved into
unoccupied military huts in St. Paul's Road, Peterborough,
Northamptonshire. Although some notices to quit were served
on Peterborough squatters, it is reported that the War Office
and the Ministry of Health have decided to take no action
against the people who have taken possession of unoccupied
Army camps in many parts of the country.
Among the families installed on the Peterborough site are
Mr. and Mrs. Harry Joseph Vines and their 3 1/2-year-old daughter
Patricia. Mr. Vines, now an inspector in a Diesel factory,
is a former Petty Officer in the Navy who won the British Empire
Medal for bringing a lifeboat safely to land after it had been
39 days in the Atlantic following the torpedoing of a troopship.
Whilst recovering from his ordeal in New York he met Caroline -
now his wife - who comes from Brooklyn.
PHOTO SHOWS:- Nissen hut wives and their children carrying water
from the camp cookhouse to their huts on the Peterborough site.
Left to right - Mrs. Helen Holmes and daughter Margaret, aged 6;
Patricia Vines, aged 3 1/2, and Mrs. Caroline Vines.
LUD August 10th 1946 PN.r.

COPYRIGHT
PLANET NEWS LTD.
3 JOHNSON'S COURT,
FLEET STREET, E.C.4.
PHONE: CENTRAL 3671/3.

activity: erecting a huge welded steel absorber column at the Stanlow oil refinery

te.text:
AN OIL REFINERY IN ENGLAND GOES INTO ACTION
29.6.51.
While the news of the Persian oil dispute still fills the
headlines, the second distillation unit in the large ex-
tensions to the great STANLOW (Cheshire) Refinery has now
been completed ahead of schedule, and is working. It treble
the refinery's output to over 3 million tons a year, and is
only part of the extensions in progress. Five further plant
including a catcracker, are yet to come into operation, and
on completion in January 1952, Stanlow will produce a com-
plete range of petroleum products from high quality petrol
the heavy fuel oil.
This picture shows a huge welded steel absorber column,
weighing 240 tons and over 170 feet long and nearly 10 feet
in diameter being erected at Stanlow refinery. Highly
specialised equipment was employed in raising this enormous
structure which was manufactured by Babcock and Wilcox at
their RENFREW works. In the back ground is the refinery's
concrete water cooling tower, largest of its kind in the
world.

COPYRIGHT PHOTO ISSUED BY
CENTRAL PRESS PHOTOS LTD.
119, FLEET STREET, LONDON, E.C.4

activity: Building a 50-ft fishing and pleasure boat inside a barn.

te.text:
50-FT. BOAT BEING BUILT IN A BARN.              AW/HT.

The largest boat ever to be built in the area is under
construction on a farm at Pevensey, Sussex.  She will
be the Eastbourne Queen, a fishing and pleasure boat,
and she is being built by Mr. R. Pragnell, of Westham.
Mr. Pragnell has had several problems to overcome -
for instance, the barn was'nt big enough to take the
boat's keel, so one end had to be knocked down and an
extension built.  And when the boat is finished, about
next May, he will have to knock down the walls of the
barn to get her out.  It will then be towed out and
transported across the fields to the water.

Photo shows-          Building the 50-ft boat in the barn
at Pevensey.  The vessel will be 13ft broad, and will
be the biggest on Eastbourne Beach.
Fox Feb 23. 49.                398848

THIS PHOTOGRAPH IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
'DAILY HERALD' ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

te.text: Industry.. Building and Construction.. Anti weather

DOMED PLASTIC HOME FOR TRADITIONAL MARKET
December 10th 1968 PAP 137154-1  (A-0)

DOMED PLASTIC HOME FOR TRADITIONAL MARKET

To make room for an overpass on the A 13 in
Essex, 150 traders from Basildon's Pitsea
market are to be rehoused in four huge
Abstracta plastic clad domes, the first
time these have been used as semi-permanent
buildings in this country.
The domes construction is the brain-child
of Danish designer, Poel Cadovius.
One of the market domes, has been half-
sprayed with concrete, nine feet upwards
from its base.
The domes are expected to remain on the new
market site between eight to ten years, and
if successful may become a permanency.
The advantage to the traders, is that
in their traditional market which was largely
in the open-air, the new venture will offer
them complete cover from the unreliable
English weather.
December 10th 1968 PAP 137154-1  (A-0)
PRESS ASSOCIATION PHOTOS
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION IN EVENING PAPERS OF
TUESDAY DECEMBER 10th 1968

activity: Alan Doyle and Anthony Woodcock loading old film reels into a furnace at the John Betts bullion firm to extract silver.

te.text:
Yesterday thousands of feet of old
film—some showing multi-million-
pound epics of the silver screen
—went up in a puff of smoke to
produce real silver for Britain.
Silver is in short supply and
expensive, at 12s. 3d. an ounce.
Which is why cast-off film from
the cinema, and T.V is sent
every day to the 200-year-old
bullion firm of John Betts.
'There the reels are burnt in a
furnace to extract their silver
content.
Yesterday it was the turn of
'Camelot,' 'The Informer' and
dozens of petrol and soap powder
advertisements to be loaded into the
furnace by Alan Doyle and Anthony
Woodcock.
On other days it could
be old 'Bootsie And
Snudge' films from T.V—
or even "blue" films.
The result each week is
30 1,000oz. ingots of silver
worth £18,000.
Director Christopher
Betts said: "We get
everything from epics
down to the mistakes
which famous actors make
and never want shown.
Security
"We have tight security
to ensure that everything
is burned and no film is
kept back for private view-
ing."
But he added: "We
recently managed to save
a David Attenborough
series which had not been
shown. The BBC cleared
it out by mistake. But one
of their men was here for
hours and managed to
save most of it.
"We reckon the aver-
age small photographer
could save £50 a year in
silver which he usually
pours down the drain or
throws away.
"One man we know now
has solid silver paper
weights from his waste so
that he can up-stage his
rivals."

screen

te.text:
PICTURE FROM THE AIR -- 111 MEN ENTOMBED IN PIT DISASTER AT
WHITEHAVEN, CUMBERLAND.

Five rescue parties fought their way through the under sea
workings of the "William Pit, Whitehaven, Cumberland, in a
search for 111 men trapped by an explosion.
Nine doctors, and ambulances summoned from as far away as
Carlisle-40 miles distant- waited at the pithead, among
shawled and weeping women.
One hundred and twenty men were in the pit when the explosion
took place. Ten of them are known to be safe, and seven of
that number remained below with the rescue parties.
PHOTO SHOWS:-- An air view of the scene of the disaster at
the William Pit, Whitehaven Cumberland. Lines of ambulances
are waiting as rescue workers and anxious relatives and friends
wait for the latest news of the rescue efforts.
And August 16th 1947 PH

te.text:
THE Association of British Chambers of Commerce has been officially rebuked over a heading on a pamphlet attacking the Labour Party's superannuation plan.
The heading included the statement
[Seal of the Association of British Chambers of Commerce: INDUSTRY COMMERCE TRANSPORT]
[Below seal: Patron Her Majesty the Queen]
that the Queen is the Association's patron.
The Association has now apologised and blacked out the phrase on the pamphlet.
Official action was taken after two Labour MPs received copies of the pamphlet and objected to the Association linking the Queen's patronage with a Party political controversy.

Coventry, Eng: In the world's largest tractor factory

te.text:
PRESS INFORMATION
Issued by
ESSO PETROLEUM COMPANY, LIMITED
36 QUEEN ANNE'S GATE, LONDON, S.W.I
TELEPHONE: WHITEHALL 5151
(Esso logo)
DATE 27th July, 1956 For Release Immediate Ref. No. 882
For additional information please refer to R. B. Sawrey-Cookson Extension 20
or after 7 p.m. telephone: WEStern 6145
OIL AND AUTOMATION
Automation has long been a feature of oil refining operations.
This photograph shows part of the control panel of the new £4 million
Fluid Catalytic Hydroformer at the Esso Refinery, Fawley, which processes
raw petrol obtained by primary distillation, and converts it into a very
high quality petrol.
Miniature instruments to record and control flow, pressure,
temperature, levels and so on, are let into the panel at positions
corresponding to those at which they operate on the plant.
The temperature console (foreground) indicates on the dials
some 200 temperature points in the plant.
The Hydroformer, capable of processing from 350,000 to
525,000 gallons a day, is operated by six men per shift. Of this
number, only one is present at all times, others only coming in
periodically to log operating conditions, as shown here.
----oO0Oo----
File - Indus - Fuel and Power - Oil - Refineries - FAWLEY.

DAILY HERALD

title: A photographic print of Gorilla
activity: Introduction of a young gorilla named Meng to a baby chimpanzee named Jacqueline at London Zoo

te.text:
A NEW HUSBAND FOR "MOINA"

The Belgian Government have presented the London Zoo
with a new husband for "Moina".  He isn't old enough
or big enough to go in with her yet, as he is only
about a year old.  "Meng", as he is called after
the village where he was found, is a sturdy and
intelligent little youngster of the Mountain mf or
Kivu race of Gorilla.  When he grows up he will be
almost twice the size of the late lamented "Mok".
Male Kivu Gorillas, when fully grown, weigh up to
600 pounds.  "Meng" is being introduced to-day to
Jacqueline", the baby Chimpanzee at the Zoo which
has been brought up on the bottle by her keepers.  It
is hoped that they will take to each other and be
company for each other until "Meng" is big enough
to put up with "Moina".

activity: an inspector examining the moulded envelope of a rubber hot water bottle during the return to peace-time production

te.text:
LONG LAST - THE RETURN OF THE RUBBER HOT WATER BOTTLE.

The big switch-over to peace-time production in the large war
factories, is now in full swing. Rubber, that vital necessity
in the manufacture of the munitions of war, has now been re-
leased for the production of a greatly needed article - the
Hot Water Bottle. Our series of pictures secured at a factory
in Streatham, shews the reversion to peace-time schedule where
a few months ago, the workers were busy on the products of war-
dinghies, anti-aircraft fuze covers, and a thousand and one
other things. Thousands of hot water bottles, are being turned
out each week, but about 25% are for export, and on the home
market, priority is given to sick people, expectant mothers etc.
At present the 'mixture' is half natural rubber and half
synthetic, and this limits the colour range. Most people prefer
red from the present selection, and many manufacturers produce
this colour only, but we are looking forward to the days when
all natural rubber can be used, and the pre-war range of colours
can return.

Photograph shows :- An inspector examining the moulded
envelope.
FOX PHOTOS JAN 15th 46. 333489.

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

activity: conveyors and external facilities of the coke-oven and by-product plant at Nantgarw

te.text:
STEPHENS OF CARDIFF.  D.H.  20-6-51.
THE COKE-OVEN AND BY-PRODUCT PLANT AT NANTGARW.
The Nantgarw plant, designed to be both functional and pleasing to the eye, is laid out amongst plants ans trees. The coke-ovens are to be fired next month and preparations are well in hand.
OPS.  The gleaming white maze of conveyors, with its brightly painted windows, will transport 1,500 tons of coal per day from the railway sidings to the ovens.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
REC: 21 JUN 1951
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY

HERE are some of the
cased-in conveyers which
will feed 1,500 tons of blended
coking coal a day to the Coal
Board's 48 new ovens at
Nantgarw, Glamorgan.

The ovens and by-products
plant, built at a cost of
£2,500,000, will be run by 140
men.

They will have a daily output
of 18,000,000 cubic feet of gas,
1,100 tons of coke, 3,000 gallons
of benzol, 16 tons of ammonia
liquid and 40 tons of tar.

Entrance to the plant is
flanked by flower beds, and tree-
lined roads run through it. Next
door is the reconstructed Nant-
garw Colliery which, in two
years, will supply the plant with
two-thirds of its coal needs.

And nearby is Treforest Trad-
ing Estate, with its neat rows
of factories.

The plant was to have been
opened by the King on July 17.
But although he has had to
cancel his Welsh visit, the ovens
will be fired on schedule. As
they heat up, there will be eight
weeks final preparation for pro-
duction.

activity: Workmen hoisting staircasing for an oil derrick construction.

te.text:
XHN)           BORING TWO MILES FOR OIL

Hundreds of men are now hard at work on the slopes of
Portsdown Hill, near Portsmouth, preparing for the
gigantic task of penetrating twice as far beneath the
surface of England as ever before. In this peaceful
spot engineers are making ready to drill to a point
10,000 feet - or nearly two miles - under the ground
in a search for oil. The hole is to be drilled with the
most modern of machinery, the work being carried out
under the supervision of expert mining engineers who
have been brought from the oilfields of Persia. Ports-
down Hill was decided on as the site for boring after a
careful survey by geologists.

Photo shows:- Workmen hoisting staircasing up the 136ft.
derrick which has been erected at Portsdown.

EVICTED FAMILY CAMP ON PAVEMENT.

LONDON : WITH THEIR BELONGINGS AROUND THEM, MR. AND

FURNITURE ON THE PAVEMENT, WHERE THEY HAVE CAMPED FOR

MR. BERNARD CLARK, 29, A £9 13s 6d A WEEK PAINTER AND HIS
FAMILY WERE EVICTED BY THE FINCHLEY COUNCIL FROM THEIR HOME
UNDER A COMPULSORY PURCHASE ORDER, AND NOW THE FAMILY CAMP
ON THE PAVEMENT. THE COUNCIL HAVE OFFERED TO PUT HIS WIFE
AND SON INTO A HOSTEL, BUT THEY HAVE REFUSED, THE COUNCIL
ALSO OFFERED TO RE-HOUSE THEM WITH MRS. CLARK'S PARENTS IN

MOTHER-IN-LAW HAD BEEN MOVED TO A ONE-BEDROOMED FLAT AND
DIDN'T WANT TO LEAVE.

11TH OCTOBER, 1957 PILS

activity: Rescue of miner Morgan Clayton via stretcher at Cortonwood Colliery.

te.text:
INLAND TELEPHOTO   YEP   LONDON BUREAU
IN 416049
"MINER SAFE" :
WOMBWELL, Yorks : Mr MORGAN CLAYTON is carried on a
stretcher by his workmates here today. Four miners, trapped
for nine and a half hours at a gas-filled coal face at
Cortonwood Colliery, died before rescue workers reached
them just before dawn today. The miners were overcome by
deadly methane gas which got into the underground workings
after the roof subsided.
At first it was hoped that the men
would be found alive but unconscious. But after rescue
workers got to them a doctor went from the pit bottom to the
seam and found them dead.
Mr Clayton was the second man to
be got out alive today.
20th June, 1961 - pn-on

te.text:
GOSPORT BUILDS MILLIONAIRE'S YACHT - FOR DOLLARS    D/ VIG

Some 60 men are at present engaged in building the largest
yacht to be made in Britain since the war, at Gosport. It
is a composite 125-ton ketch, with a 70-foot waterline,
ordered by 45-year-old American tobacco millionaire, Mr.
Richard J. Reynolds. The craft is built mainly of teak on
steel frames, with stern timbers of Mahogany. It is expected
to be ready for launching by June, will cost about £60,000
which Mr. Reynolds will pay in dollars.

PHOTO SHOWS: At Camper and Nicholson's yard at Gosport,
Dennis Sears (left) and Cyril Palmer are seen laying the
deck on the forehead of the new yacht, the 785 as it is
called in the sheds.

WORLD'S FIRST CATAMARAN DRILLING VESSEL DEVELOPED.

Latest addition to a series of unique international
floating drilling rigs is an unusual 278 ft. twin hulled
catamaran. Called the E.W. THORNTON the vessel is capable
of boring more than 4 miles beneath the ocean bed when in
600 ft. of water.
Shape and size of the 6,000 ton craft is said to make
it an "engineering marvel" in the field of floating oil
drilling rigs. Built to withstand rough seas, it is held
in place by eight 10-ton anchors to prevent drifting.

under its own power at speeds up to 12 knots and carries
a crew of 86. The catamaran has a 142 ft. (115 ton)

title: A photographic print of Industry, Stone

activity: Men lowering a large stone from seasoning piles in an underground limestone mine.

te.text:
MINING STONE ON WILTSHIRE BORDER.      CH/BU

The OOLITIC Limestone or Bath stone quarries at Corsham and Box
on the Wiltshire border near Bath are unique in that the stone
is quarried from a mine 100 feet underground. The tunnels extend
for miles beneath the hillside and in one instance the shaft
enters the ground at one side of the hill and comes out three
miles away.  The stone is cut by means of huge saws and lifted
out by cranes and many of the stones weigh 12 tons. All stone
quarried in winter is left in mine until warmer days. Temper-
ature in mine is about 56 degrees all year round.

Photo shows- Like the ruins of some ancient city- Men lowering
a large stone from one of the immense piles which have been
standing for seasoning.
FOX March 2nd. 33.

activity: Three members of a housing association building bungalows on an estate.

te.text:
KENT PIONEERS BUILD THEIR OWN HOMES. MJH/RS.

On a housing estate in Hawes Lane Beckenham (Kent) men can
be seen working by floodlights on bungalows in various stages
of completion, sometimes up till ten o'clock at night. The
reason for this keen enthusiasm is that the men are working on their
own homes, or homes for their friends. Calling themselves, the
Beckenham Housing Association, this band of 25 pioneers includes
men from many trades - only a few are builders, the rest are
clerks, shopkeepers, cahiers, a post office engineer, etc, etc.,
but they are fast learning the art of house building as they work
with a will to erect their own homes. Order of priority is worked
out by friendly agreement and as each man works on a home for
his friend, he looks forward to the day when work will begin on
his own home.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS: Three members of the Beckenham Housing
Association seen working on one of the bungalows on the Hawes Lane
estate. They are (left to right) COLIN MCDONALD; FRED
MATTINGLY: and LESLIE COOK. The men work on the estate in the
evenings when they have finished their own day's work, and at
weekends.
FOX PHOTOS MARCH 3RD. 1955. 515053.

FOX PHOTOS LTD.

activity: Construction of the Ford factory at Halewood showing buildings in skeleton form.

te.text:
10 PER CENT OF WORKING TIME LOST ON FORD'S FACTORY.

It seems that Ford chief Sir Patrick Hennessy's accusation against the Trades Unions that up until October 30th, 81,000 working days were lost on the £30 million factory at Halewood, near Liverpool, because of labour disputes. The Company has just issued a statement in reply to Union protests against Sit Patrick's allegations disclosing that in fact, out of a possible 810,972 working days, 51,016 were lost because of weather, and a further 84,226 because of disputes. This loss of more than 10 percent of working time, has put construction on the 346 acre site way nehind schedule. Much of the site still resembles a battle field and many of the buildings are still in skeleton form.

KEYSTONE/JP/16590

KEYSTONE
PRESS AGENCY LTD.
4-7, RED LION COURT,
LONDON, E.C.4.

activity: Ex-miners manufacturing miniature pedal cars in a Pengam factory.

te.text:
KEN LAUDER          D.H.          15.2.56
MINERS MAKE MOTOR CARS.
Miners from the Welsh collieries are making
motor cars at Pengam (Monmouthshire), twelve
miles north of Cardiff.  But the motor cars
which they turn out from their clean, modern
factory are the kind that bring a sparkle into
the eyes of children.  For the factory was
started by the Austin Motor Company to employ
men who had left the mines, disabled by "dust
disease".  The miners, now 200 of them, have
taken so well to making the miniature pedal cars,
that they have produced 17,000 since the factory
was opened.  Thousands of these have been exported
to the U.S.A, Africa, Argentine, Canada and
Palestine.  Conditions of work at the factory are
supervised by a doctor.
O.P.S. 3-years-old Christopher Evans, a strictly
unofficial test driver, is watched by some of the
ex-miners who make the cars, which are the
production of their 'big brother' Austins. L. to
R. Alf Kent, 53 (from Grosfaen Colliery), Herbert
Price, 41, (from Markhal Colliery), Elwyn
Stephens, 43, (Bargoed Colliery) and Sydney Hoskins,
50 (Pengam).

FILE- INDUS. - FUEL + POWER - COAL
MINERS - WELFARE

PORTABLE HOUSE FOR £288.
Portable house tents made of nylon tarpaulin which
can withstand gale force winds and freezing temper-

beach cottages suitable for housing 32 persons. They
cost £288, and can easily be carried by a station wagon.

te.text: Industry - Fuel and Power - Electricity - Power Stns - BANKSIDE.

244482   SKI
BANKSIDE POWER STATION: PRODUCTION GETS UNDER WAY
London: An industrial project which has aroused
much controversy from the time of its conception
has just gone into operation.
It is the Bankside Power Station, at which
the first 60,000-kilowatt turbo-alternator of about
80,000 horse-power, has started to supply electricity.
The project was allowed on condition that oil and not
coal was to be burned. Other conditions which had to
be observed were that the building must be set back
far enough from the Thames so as not to interfere with
the projected road and promenade.
Opposition to the Power station was so strong that
in January, 1947, a public inquiry was held, with the
result that the scheme was given Government sanction.
On completion the Bankside Power Station will
comprise four 60,000-kilowatt generating sets, the
oil consumption at full load (16-hour day) being
67 tons an hour, consuming in one winter's day about
850 tons.

te.text:
BRITAIN'S ROLLERS MAKE THE ROADS OF THE WORLD.
July 1946
Britain has long been famous in the production of road
rollers and other types of road construction machinery,
and the "Invicta" horse of the products of Messrs Aveling-
Barford of Grantham is to be seen even in the most out
of the way spots of the globe. The latest order received
by this firm is for a million pounds-worth of road rollers
destined for use in all parts of India. Besides this huge
order, they have others in hand worth threefold for the
supply of machinery to all parts - from Iceland in the
north to New Zealand in the south, and only lack of labour
and further supplies of raw materials prevents the accept-
ance of additional contracts. This work has not been gained
by sitting at home - their representatives have travelled
the world and the result of their missions is seen today in
the increased activity in the Grantham factory, as illustrated
by the accompanying pictures :-

activity: Boys from a children's home auctioning their pet pig at Saffron Walden market.

te.text: FILE - PIGS - DH ONLY. INDUS - AGRIC.
FOR CONTACTS. SEE CHILDREN WITH ANIMALS.

GREAVES   D.H.   20.12.55.
A LITTLE PIG GOES TO MARKET.
The boys at the Church of England Home at Ashdon,
near Saffron Walden, Essex had a baby pig given to
them. They built a sty and have looked after it for
the past five months. They named it Biology and made
a real pet of it, but it has now grown into a fine
porker of 8 and a half score pounds. Today they got
up at 6-30am. washed and powdered Biology and took
her to Saffron Walden market. It was auctioned and
and brought the boys fourteen guineas, they now hope
to extend their piggy activities.
O.P.S. Some of the boys say good bye to Biology
at the pig sales.

PROPERTY OF
DAILY HERALD
PLEASE RETURN
TO
ART LIBRARY
21 DEC 1955

BIOLOGY the pig woke
early yesterday. She
had to be washed, pow-
dered and combed. For it
was market day at Saffron
Walden,
Biology, you see, is a fine
13-stone porker raised by
the 20 boys at the Church
of England home at Ash-
don, Essex. She was given
to them five months ago.
Ever since, they have been
fattennig her for the
Christmas market.
The boys turned up in
their school lunch break to
see Biology auctioned. And
before the bidding began,
they gave her a final
fattening sweet.
She fetched 14 guineas.

Devonport, Devon: Mr Percy Rickard, aged 68, points

activity: Large motor-boat nearing completion at a dockyard wharf.

te.text:
LONDON'S BIGGEST SPEED BOAT NEARS COMPLETION.

One of the world's largest motor-boats and the biggest ever built
in a London dockyard is nearing completion at Ferry Wharf, Isleworth.
The speed boat is 105-foot long and fitted with four 1,700
horse-power Bristol aircraft engines. With a cruising speed of
38 knots, she will be capable of making an Atlantic crossing
in three days.
Equipment includes hot and cold water supply, an electric cooker
and a refrigerator.
This craft was originally ordered two years ago together with
five others which were planned for air-sea rescue work in the
Atlantic. Only this one is being completed, work on the others
having been suspended after the defeat of Germany.
PHOTO SHOWS:- The motor-boat nearing completion at Ferry Wharf,
Isleworth, near London.

ROGER McPHEE talks to hens. He
talks to them about the weather
and politics and sport: he was say-
ing yesterday that his four Rhode
Island Reds, June, Henrietta, Mary
and Flossie, have become inter-
ested in football. Mr. McPhee,
aged 24, a pet shop manager, of
Hills Road, Cambridge, has noted
that eggs produced by his hens
tend to have double yolks. The
reason may, of course, be that he
has put the hens on a special diet.
But Mr. McPhee prefers to think
that is not the real reason. A man
likes to believe he can talk a
woman into anything.

Henrietta, Mary and Flossie - he discusses the weather and politics and
feed them on a diet of crushed oats, flaked maize, rabbit pellets and racing
pigeon feed, in return the hens usually lay double yolked egges.

Flying to North America  under armed escort
on Thursday (August 17th) is one of the most
valuable consignments of gold  ever to leave this

makers (Adie Brothers Birmingham  ) to  London
Airport.   Heaviest  piece of the service is the tray
- weighing  220 ounces - probably the largest  piece of
18ct gold assayed at the Birmingham Assay  Office
since its  opening.

on the  tea pot of the  £9000   GOLD SERVICE
which going on tour  of 25 cities in Canada

bowls and a dish produced at the pottery have been

take advantage of the facilities provided - potters'

21.10.65.

WESSEX 60 HANDED OVER TO BRISTOW HELICOPTERS.

A Westland WESSEX 60 G-ATBY, was
handed over to Bristow Helicopters at Westland
Heliport, Battersea today. A member of the
Air Holdings Group and an Associate of British United
Airways, Bristow Helicopters operate Europe's largest
helicopter fleet, totalling more than 60 machines.
Since 1952, the Company have built up unrivalled
experience in operating support services for offshore
drilling in many parts of the world, including the
Caribbean, Iran, the Arabian Gulf, Nigeria, the
Antarctic and the North Sea. Bristow Helicopters
have four Wessex 60's on order, for use on offshore
support services in the North Sea, under their many
contracts with oil Companies operating in this area.
Ten of the eleven Co. companies which have decided to use
helicopters, have awarded contracts to Bristow Helicopters.

KEYSTONE PHOTO SHOWS:- The aircraft flies off
on delivery to Redhill, after today's handing-
over ceremony at Westland Heliport, Battersea.
H/Keystone WES/785033

COPYRIGHT PHOTOGRAPH

JOHN TOPHAM,
1, BIRCHWOOD AVENUE,

PLOUGHING IN LEEKS
            A view of part of the excellent
crop of Leeks at Childs Farm, Cooling (between Gravesend
and Rochester), Kent - farmed by Messrs. J. Edmonds and Sons Ltd.
            Nearly twenty acres are now being ploughed
in since the leeks are unsaleable. Markets abroad have
been tried with success. The farmer says that these
scenes are the result of excess quantities of imported
onions being allowed in the country, causing a complete
lack of trade for the home grown produce.
            It is no use letting the leeks
stay in the ground any longer, for the next crop (potatoes)
is due for planting.
            The loss to the producer and farm
worker, financially, is very heavy.
24417       7/2/49 John Topham, Sidcup, Kent.

te.text:
LN 266267          DAW          LONDON BUREAU

AS THE SHIP TAKES SHAPE SO
 WILL THE DOCK

NEWPORT, MON. The first British shipyard in
which vessels are being built in dry dock and
under cover is somewhat unique in that
work is being carried out on the first of two
3,000-ton ships while the dock itself is in the
process of construction. Thus, as the size of
the ship increases, so will the dock. If everything
goes according to plan, they will, by the time
the ship is built, be able to open the dock gate
and allow the vessel to float out on the 40 ft.
tide. The dock, which was opened in November
by Sir David Maxwell Fyfe, Home Secretary and
Minister for Welsh Affairs, is situated at the
mouth of the River Usk. The two ships ordered
are both wood pulp carriers for a Canadian company,
and sections of them, after being prefabricated
in a number of shops, are lowered into position
in the dock.
PHOTO SHOWS: The flat-bottom keel of the first of
two 3,000-ton ships being laid in the half-finished
dry dock.
                                17th February 1954 PN-b

te.text:
Sept. 20th. '65.
Harvesting by Headlights.
The drone of the tractor engine can be heard well into the night
down West Horsley way as Farmer Percy Yates and his men gather
in the late harvest by the light of the tractor headlights.
It is a ten hour day starting at eleven, and finishing after nine
the morning, and the bad summer with so much rain is the reason for
the night work.
Since the middle of August Mr. Yates has been working on one hundred and
eleven acres, he now has only fifteen acres left to do, and prov-
iding this Indian Summer goes on the harvest will be completed.
O.P.S. Peter Oxley a farm student directs the headlights of his tractor
for Combine Operator Reg Williams and farm student John Walker
on the International Harvester, working late into the night at
Space Farm West Horsley owned by Farmer Percy Yates.

activity: Arthur Capps' design for a self-heating and self-lit bungalow powered by a windmill and heat pump.

te.text:
By Alan Dick
WOULD you like a central-
heated bungalow with no
coal or electricity bills, no
water rate, and free H and C
with all mod con? Then Mr.
Arthur Capps is your man.
Mr. Capps, a family man in the
forties, works in the radio depart-
ment of the Royal Aircraft Estab-
lishment at Farnborough, Hamp-
shire, and has a cottage at
Crowthorne, Berks.
With the help of his wife and
15-year-old son Martin he has
designed a new-world bungalow
generating its own heat and light.
Mr. Capps says he has found
how to make a simple windmill
provide free running hot and cold
water, heat for cooking, central
heating and electric light, and all
at no greater cost to build than
an ordinary home.
From the air
His idea is to use a windmill-
driven heat pump to extract heat
from the air during the hot
weather and to store it under-
ground for use in the cold weather
(and any other time).
The job will be done by low-
pressure steam, got by trickling
water down the inside of the wind-
mill post so that heat from the
air is absorbed and turned into
steam.
This steam is compressed to 500
or 600 degrees Fahrenheit super-
heat, passed through a brick
rubble heat reservoir to absorb
the superheat, and passed on to
water and soil reservoirs which will
absorb the latent heat.
Lighting comes from a small
steam turbine dynamo, water from
a small well fed by rain from the
roof and sent to the upper tank
by a windmill-worked pump.
Said Mr. Capps yesterday: " I
hope to build my bungalow on a
plot I have bought."
... 2 hours

te.text:
BRITAIN'S "WINE CELLAR" - THE LONDON DOCKS.     MJH/HT.

The British people are drinking more wine these days, proved
by the fact that so far this year, with the festive season
still to come, Britain's wine consumption is 10 per cent
higher than last year.  Sherry is almost back to pre-war
popularity - this year's consumption has risen to 80 per cent
of the 1939 level.  This rising demand means that the London Docks
are becoming more and more Britain's wine cellar with the bonded
vaults and warehouses doing a "roaring trade".  This country
still imports most wine from France, Spain and Portugal, followed
by Germany, South Africa, Italy and Australia.

PHOTOGRAPH SHOWS:       Draining off from casks of sherry which

bottling.

LONDON : WITH THEIR BELONGINGS AROUND THEM, MR. AND

FURNITURE ON THE PAVEMENT, WHERE THEY HAVE CAMPED FOR

activity: Tenant protest and living conditions at Beaconsfield Buildings slums.

te.text:
IN SOME WAYS Beaconsfield
Buildings, just a short bus ride
from the glitter of Piccadilly
Circus, could be considered a
showplace.
For to film producers at least, the
grey-bricked, five-storey blocks of flats
seem to have an irresistable fascina-
tion.
There was Max Bygraves in Cry From
the Streets, and Spare the Rod and
Spoil the Child. There was Joe Brown
in What a Crazy World. And Jess
Conrad in The Boys.
Each finding in the rows of miserable
flats—known without affection as The
Crumbles—the perfect setting for a film
about slums.
For today Beaconsfield Buildings has
about as much in common with the
affluent gadget world of 1964 as it did
when Prime Minister Disraeli laid the
foundation stone in 1875.
The plumbing is still Victorian. There
are few separate kitchens, few bath-
rooms, and landing lavatories shared by
between five and eight families.

On Sunday 200 of the 440 tenants
marched five miles from the flats in
Randall's Road, near King's Cross, to the
Chelsea home of Housing Minister Sir
Keith Joseph. To ask him to pull The
Crumbles down.
Their case? Well, it can be found in
the story of just three families.
CASE ONE: Mrs. Bridget Welsh, aged 45,
wife of a labourer, lives in three rooms
and a partitioned kitchen at £1 14s. 2d.
a week. Her flat is spotless.
She said: "Six weeks ago my girl
Geraldine—she's 10—caught dysentry.
Not from our lavatory because I clean it
constantly, and not from her school be-
cause she was the only one.
"I'm afraid she caught it round the
Buildings—from open dustbins, bad, smelly
drains, or dirty walls."
CASE TWO: Mrs. Bridget Sullivan, aged
26, wife of a factory worker, with children
Michael, 3, Theresa, one, in two rooms, no
kitchen, at £1 6s. 10d. a week. Her flat
is spotless.

DAILY HERALD
BY G. BARHAM

te.text:
STEPHENS, CARDIFF 8.11.51
LINKING OF MARDY AND BWLLFA COLLIERIES BY TUNNEL
OPS. Scene on the Mardy side after the last charge had
been blown and the men who have been on the job saw the
results of their labours. With a rush of air and a
shower of rubble a small hole appeared. It was just
big enough for a man to crawl through but a lot of
rock had to be moved from the Bwllfa side before it
could be made safe.

STEPHENS, CARDIFF 8.11.51
Tonight saw the great moment of climax after two
years work to link Mardy and Bwllfa collieries by a
tunnel 400 yds below Darren Montain, which stands
between the two pits - one in Rhondda Fach - the other
in the Aberdare Valley. This is part of a £4 million
scheme to develop Mardy colliery. The link was made
under the heart of the mountain dead on time, and
not a foot out.
OPS. Scene on the Mardy side after the last charge had

U.S. REPLACEMENT CAMP.
OPS 2.  Before the men are billeted and fed, their
indivisual papers and records will be undergoing
processing, or sorting, in the Depot Classification
abd personnel offices. Lt. Werner N.Snow, represent-
ing the Depot Classification Officer, and his men
receive from the Troop Train Commander the
individual records of every enlisted man on the
train. Control of records is so vital to efficient
control and assignment of troops in motion that
this transfer on the platform is the third step in
the sequence. At the port of debarcation the
Depot Escort Officer has seen to it that all records
are gathered in the Train Commander's compart-
ment.  The weapon slung on the Train Commander's
back is the .30 calibre carbine. An offensive
weapon, it replaces the essentially defensive
pistol for all ranks through Major.

te.text:
EXCLUSIVE CENTRAL PRESS FEATURE
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION THURSDAY'S EVENINGS, July 24th.
SILK WORMS THAT HELP BRITAIN'S EXPORTS
A small but very important aid to Britain's export trade is
being given by about six million silkworms which are being
reared at Lullingstone Castle Silk Farm, run by ZOE, LADY
HART DYKE, near Eynsford, Kent.
The aim and object of the farm is to develop and assist
production of raw silk in this country, the Dominions, and
the Colonies, and what started off as a girl's hobby, de-
veloped on a business footing in 1932, is now a flourishing
industry housed in one of Britain's ancient homes.
The Lullingstone silkworms are known all over the world
for millions of them have been exported, and it was from
their silk that the Coronation Robes of the Queen and the
Princesses were made. This brought the farm an international
reputation, and visitors from all corners of the globe are
taken over the farm during their visits.
One of the great difficulties now being experienced at
Lullingstone is the lack of mulberry leaves on which the
worms feed, for the eighteen acre plantation of mulberry
trees is only producing about half the number of leaves re-
quired by the six million tiny mouths.
It is interesting to note that the method of using the silk
cocoon for spinning and weaving was first known in China
at least 3,000 years B.C. It was James I who endeavoured to
encourage silkworm rearing in this country by ordering the
importation and planting of thousands of mulberry trees, but
the Royal scheme was a failure. George I then took a keen
interest in the silk industry and in 1718 he granted a
patent to a certain John Appleton for silkworm rearing.
The picture shows one of the assistants at Lullingstone Castle
feeding a batch of silk worms with mulberry leaves. At this
stage the worms are about three weeks old.

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY

te.text:
NEW CRANE THAT DOUBLES SPEED OF HOUSE
BUILDING        8-11-51
________________________________________
Britain is now using a new kind of crane,
designed at the Government Building Research
Station at Watford, Hertfordshire, which
should double the speed of house building.
It is based on a similar device in use on
the Continent and should help to overcome
the heavy building leeway. The crane runs
on rails but the jib, instead of rising
diagonally from the base, works horizontally
from the upright structure. It enables materials
not only to be lifted vertically but moved
horizontally across the building site to
the spot where the craftsmen need them.
Instead of bricklayers clambering up ladders
with a dozen bricks in a hod, the crane will
deliver 160 to 180 bricks at a time and
place them by the side of the bricklayer.

I.N.P. PHOTO SHOWS:- The crane delivering
bricks on the spot beside bricklayers
at work on a Camberwell building site,
London.

Picture by J. Davies.

activity: Introduction of a young gorilla named Meng to a baby chimpanzee named Jacqueline at London Zoo.

te.text:
SAIDMAN.                                 10.8.38.
A New Husband for "Moina"
The Belgian Government have presented the London
Zoo with a new husband for "Moina".  He isn't
old enough or big enough to go with her yet
as he is only about a year old.  "Meng" as he
is called after the village where he was found,
is a sturdy and intelligent little youngster of
the Mountain or Kivu race of Gorilla.  When he
grows up he will be almost twice the size of the
late lamented "Mok".     Male Kivu Gorillas when
fully grown weigh up to 600 pounds.  "Meng"
is being introduced today to "Jacqueline"
the baby Chimpanzee at the Zoo which has been
brought up on the bottle by her keepers.  It
is hoped that they will take to each other
and be company for each other until "Meng"
is big enough to be put with "Moina".

XXXXXXX V.87903
LONDON'S NEW HEALTH CENTRE AT WOODBERRY DOWN.
Last May, the London County Council approved proposals
for carrying out some of its new duties under the
National Health Service Act, 1946. One of these
proposals was to erect a comprehensive Health
Centre on the L.C.C. Woodberry Down Estate at Stoke
Newington. Next Tuesday, 25th January,
the Council will be asked by its Health Committee to
approve a capital estimate of £187,275 for the
building of the new Health Centre. It will be the
first of its kind in London, and the first in the
whole country to be approved by the Minister of
Health. Under one roof will be brought for the first
time ante and post-natal clinics, a child welfare
clinic, a school treatment centre, other local Health
services and general practitioner and dental services.
Picture shows:- a model of the new Centre at County
Hall, Westminster today (Fri).

early yesterday. She
had to be washed, pow-
dered and combed. For it

to them five months ago.

fattennig her for the

fattening sweet.

te.text:
MARCHING
MINERS IN
PROTEST
FORTY THOUSAND South Wales miners, many
with their wives and children, blocked the main
streets in Cardiff for nearly
an hour yesterday during
their annual gala march.
Most of the banners
carried by the marchers
protested against the train-
ing of German troops in
Pembrokeshire.
Later, at a mass meeting
addressed by two M.P.s,
Mr. Michael Foot and Miss
Jennie Lee, a resolution was
passed calling for the with-
drawal of all troops and
armaments by all nations
from military bases abroad
and in particular the with-
drawal of German troops
from Wales.
Speaking of Government
plans for the coal industry,
Mr. Foot said they wanted
to divide the industry into
districts competing against
each other.
" This is the sort of ruth-
less competition which was
largely responsible for the
devastation suffered in the
mining areas in the years
gone by," he said.
Four uniformed nurses sat
alongside the main speakers.
Mr. Will Whitehead, presi-
dent of the South Wales
miners, said:
" We have said that if the
nurses want our help we
shall be there with them."

File 'V' Aviation Post War - Brit Air Liners - Bristol Brabazon.

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION MONDAY, Oct 21st.
ENGLISH VILLAGE MAKES WAY FOR GIANT PLANE
20.10.46.
Sacrificed to the cause of progress, the village of 
CHARLTON, near Bristol, England, has been demolished to make 
room for the runway spacious enough to allow the first take-
off of the giant Bristol "Brabazon" air liner prototype 
now under construction at the famous works. A vast assembly 
hall is also being built because she cannot be put together 
in any existing building. 
Features of the great aircraft are - wing span 230ft, height 
50ft at rudder, and length 177ft. All-up weight 125 tons, 
and sleeping berths for 80 passengers for night travel. It 
is designed to fly direct between London and New York or 
Montreal, and gas turbines in the wings accessible during 
flight will give her a speed of 350 mph at 35,000ft and her 
range will be 5,000 miles. The picture shows a nose view of 
the Bristol "Brabazon" prototype in its nest of jigs and 
scaffolding. Workmen give an idea of its size.

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD"
AND MUST BE RETURNED
UNDAMAGED.

DESTROYING TWENTY ACRES OF LEEKS
			The tractor and discs dice up part
of a good twenty acre crop of leeks - prior to ploughing
back into the land as unsaleable, at Cooling, Kent.
			All markets have been tried - even
abroad - but nobody wants leeks.
			Since the land is wanted for planting
out early potatoes the plough must get to work - with
a resultant heavy financial loss to the producer and
farm worker.
			The farmer, Messrs. J. Edmonds and
Sons Ltd., say that these scenes are the result of
excess quantities of imported onions being allowed into
the country, causing a complete lack of trade for the
home grown produce.

te.text:
FOR FIRST PUBLICATION TUESDAY'S EVENINGS 2.7.46.

BRITAIN'S ROLLERS MAKE THE ROADS OF THE WORLD.
July 1946
Britain has long been famous in the production of road
rollers and other types of road construction machinery,
and the "Invicta" horse of the products of Messrs Aveling-
Barford of Grantham is to be seen even in the most out
of the way spots of the globe. The latest order received
by this firm is for a million pounds worth of road rollers
destined for use in all parts of India. Besides this huge
order, they have others in hand worth threefold for the
supply of machinery to all parts - from Iceland in the
north to New Zealand in the south, and only lack of labour
and further supplies of raw materials prevents the accept-
ance of additional contracts. This work has not been gained
by sitting at home - their representatives have travelled
the world and the result of their missions is seen today in
the increased activity in the Grantham factory, as illustrated
by the accompanying pictures : -

Front rollers of "GD" ten-ton roller being packed
ready for export.
File Industries Road Maintenance Machinery x Filed Rollers

23. 1. 56.

MAKING NEW RIGGING FOR NELSON'S FLAGSHIP "VICTORY"

A team of men and women have started work at Chatham
to make a complete new rigging for Nelson's Flagship,
"VICTORY". They are working in the same timber-built
rope "walks" used by the men who refitted Victory for
Trafalgar after she had been five years in the Medway
as a prison hospital ship. The work is being carried
out at Chatham's Ropery - the Admiralty's only rope-
making establishment. Methods of making the rope are
almost the same as in the days of Nelson, except that
women are employed in some of the operations, now done
by machines.
PHOTO SHOWS A view looking down the rope "walk"
which is 1,128 feet in length. It is
here that the twisted strands are put
through the final stages to complete
the rope-making.

te.text:
MAKING BASKETS FOR THE FRUIT SEASON.  E. M./MAE.

There is a big demand for fruit baskets from the orchard
districts at this time and Severnside basket makers are
working long hours to try and meet it.  Foreign competition
has, of recent years, had a discouraging effect on the basket-
making trade which, in this district, has been carried on as
a family art throughout the years.  The withies from which
the baskets are made grow on the banks of the river and after
two or three years drying, are boiled in special outdoor
boilers to make them supple.  One of the "pot hampers" as
these fruit baskets are called, takes about one hour and a
half to make and will stand several years rough usage.

Photo shows:- Mr. Venfield, who is carrying on the work of
his father, making "Pot hampers".

te.text:
LN 294440         DAW         LONDON BUREAU
LONDON'S NEW SKYSCRAPERS
LONDON :  PHOTO SHOWS :-  A NEW ELEVEN-STORY BLOCK OF
FLATS ON THE EDGE OF WIBLEDON COMMON, LONDON.
PLANET NEWS FEATURE SERVICE 1955       PN-N

LN 294440 - 294443    DAW         LONDON BUREAU
LONDON'S NEW SKYSCRAPERS
LONDON :  LONDONERS ARE GRADUALLY LEARNING HOW TO SCRAPE
SKIES AND LIKE IT. BLOCKS OF FLATS 10, 12 AND EVEN 14
STORIS HIGH ARE RISING ON THE EDGES OF RICHMOND PARK,
PUTNEY HEATH, WIMBLEDON COMMON AND WANDSWORTH COMMON.
SOME ARE ALREADY FINISHED AND THE TENANTS HAVE MOVED IN.
THERE NEW HOMES ARE A STRIKING AND IMPRESSIVE SIGHT -
EXCEPT TO OLD RESIDENTS WHOSE TWO AND THREE-STORY HOUSES
ARE OVERLOOKED BY THESE TOWERING MINIATURE SKYSCRAPERS.
THE NEW BUILINGS DON'T JUST DISFIGURE THE PLEADANT LANDSCAPE
THAT USED TO BE ON THEIR DOORSTEPS. THEY OBLITERATE IT.
IT IS HARD LUCK ON THE PEOPLE OF ROEHAMPTON AND WIMBLEDON.
BUT LONDONERS MUST LIVE SOMEWHERE. THERE CAN BE NO COMPLAIN
AGAINST THE BUILDINGS THEMSELVES. THEY ARE DESIGNED TO
INCLUDE THE BEST ELEMENTS IN MODERN ARCHITECTURAL STRUCTURE.
THEY ARE BEAUTIFUL EXAMPLES OF STYLE AND INSIDE ARE
COMFORTABLE AND EMINENTLY LIVABLE-IN. AND THE LONDON
COUNTY COUNCIL ARE BUILDING THEM IN SETTINGS ABOUT WHICH
THERE CAN BE NO COMPLAINT. £4,500,000 IS BEING SPENT ON
15 BLOCKS OF THESE FLATS AS PART OF THE ROEHAMPTON
DEVELOPMENT SCHEME, AND MORE FOR HUNDRED-FOOT STRUCTURES IN
OTHER AREAS. IT IS ALSO EXPECTED THAT WHEN THE SLUM
CLEARANCE PROJECTS GET UNDER WAY, THESE SKYSCRAPERS CAN BE
BUILT IN CLEARED AREAS NEARER TO THE HEART OF LONDON, THUS
HELPING TO SOLVE THE URGENT AND CRITICAL REHOUSING PROBLEM
IN AREAS WHERE LAND IS SCARCE.

FIRST CONSIGNMENT OF EMPIRE FLOUR FROM PORT CHURCHILL

The first consignment of Empire flour and grain from the new
Port Churchill at Hudson Bay, Canada, is now being unlaoded
from the S.S. " Pennyworth " at the Millenium Mills, Royal
Albert Docks. Some sacks of flour as well as grain are being
unloaded so that Port Churchill now supplies Britain with the
freshest flour as the sea passage from London to the new grain
port is the nearest in the world.

grain elevators unloading into the waiting barges.

Kingston, Eng: The first of Britain's 25 new power
stations - the 5 1/4 million sterling project at Kingston-

activity: Rescue of five miners from a flooded pit via bucket lift.

te.text:
HERALD REPORTERS     LYDBROOK, Glos., Thursday
FIVE miners, the last of 150 trapped in a flooded pit,
were tonight hoisted 130 yards up an old air shaft
in the Forest of Dean by a hastily-rigged bucket-and-
winch lift.
These five, who had been
"exploring" disused workings
for coal that could be worked,
had fought their way to that
air shaft, through water at
times neck-high, for seven
hours.
The rest of the 150, who were
working in the Arthur and Edward
Pit when the water swept in, were
hauled up the ordinary pit shaft
in the cage.
People from this mining hamlet
cheered the five wildly. Pit de-
puties held a final count, ticking
off the names on a list: Frank
Bradley, Oswald Simmonds, Ernie
Barnfield, Bert Sims, Tom Main-
waring. . .

UP to safety in the bucket-
and-winch lift comes 67-
year-old Bert Sims—one of the
last five of 150 miners who were
trapped in the flooded pit.

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

 In a rural setting, a peer's former home, is one of the least 
 known departments of the Admiralty - the Compass Observatory 
 at Ditton Park, near Slough, Bucks, where nearly 100 delicately 
 fingered work-people may be found industriously pulling compasses

activity: Miss A. Hewitt 'banding in' during a hop stringing competition in Kent.

te.text:
XH)           KENT HOP STRINGING COMPETITION

Believed to be the only contest of its kind in the world
the annual hop stringing competition, organised by The
Weald of Kent Ploughing Match Association, took place
to-day at Spitzbrook, Collier Street, Kent.  About 40
Kentish farmworkers, all experts in hop stringing, and
many of them coming from families which have worked in
the hop gardens for generations, took part.  The
stringer's job is to prepare hop gardens for the next
crop by putting up a complicated pattern of strings
which the hops can climb.  He works with a pole 10 feet
long, guiding the string (drawn from a bag slung over
his shoulder) from hooks in the ground to others hanging
on wires overhead.      He is followed by a "bander in"
(usually female) who binds together the groups of
vertical strings comprising a "hill."  In the
competition, each stringer completes a "cant" of 200
hills.  Some 40 miles of string are used in the
process.  Competitors score points for speed, neatness
and economy in the use of string.  The object of the
competition is to stimulate interest in the craft and
to encourage ability in a highly skilled branch of
agricultural work.

Photo shows:-  Miss A. Hewitt banding in for Mr. B.
King during the competition.

X File - Aviation - Post War "Bristol Brabazon"
FILE INDUSTRY

THE BRISTOL TYPE 167 LOW-WING CANTILEVER MONOPLANE -
SOMETIMES UNOFFICIALLY REFERRED TO AS THE BRABAZON I.

Picture shows:- the Zeppelin-like fuselage of the
giant plane under construction at the Bristol
Aeroplane Company's works at Bristol.
S/P
SUPPLIED L.N.A.
V. 39798

BRITAIN'S BIGGEST LAND PLANE.

The BRISTOL TYPE 167 low wing cantilever monoplane,
sometimes unofficially referred to as the BRABAZON I,
is the biggest land plane yet to be built by the
British aircraft industry and is now taking shape in the
Bristol Aeroplane Company's factory at Filton, Bristol.
Estimated to cost £4,000,000 the 167 is being
built solely for flight development work and is expected
to fly in the early summer of 1947.
The aircraft with an all up weight of 285,000 lbs,
- approximately 126 tons - will have a maximum level
speed of more than 300 m.p.h. at 25,000 feet, a cruising
speed of 250 m.p.h., at 25,000 feet, and a still air
range of 5,000 miles.

te.text:
Please return to
ART LIBRARY DAILIES OF

FOR FIRST PUBLICATION WEDNESDAY 23RD SEPTEMBER 1964

TWO SLIPWAYS NEEDED TO BUILD BRITAIN'S
BIGGEST TANKER EVER.
G. 9633 SEPTEMBER 1964.
ERF.
THE CONSTRUCTION OF BRITAIN'S FIRST 100,000-TON
TANKER, WHICH IS BEING BUILT FOR BRITISH PETROLEUM,
IS NOW WELL UNDER WAY, AND SHE IS DUE TO BE LAUNCHED
FROM THE VICKERS-ARMSTRONGS YARD AT BARROW-IN-FURNESS
EARLY NEXT YEAR.
THE NEW SHIP IS THE FIRST OF TWO
100,000-TONS DEADWEIGHT TANKERS BEING BUILT FOR
BP. TANKER COMPANY - THE SECOND IS UNDER CONSTRUCTION
AT SWAN HUNTER AND WIGHAM RICHARDSON'S YARD ON THE TYNE.
BP'S NEW 100,000-TON TANKER WILL BE 180 FEET IN BREADTH
917'-6" FEET OVERALL IN LENGTH AND HAVE A SUMMER DRAUGHT
OF 49 FEET. ALL THE MACHINERY WILL BE INSTALLED COMPLETE
PRIOR TO LAUNCHING AND IT WILL BE THE GREATEST-EVER
LAUNCHING WEIGHT AT BARROW. AFTER LAUNCHING, ONLY
A FEW WEEKS WILL BE REQUIRED TO PREPARE THE NEW TANKER
FOR FINAL TRIALS.
IN ORDER TO ACCOMMODATE THE GREATER WIDTH
OF THE NEW VESSEL, TWO EXISTING BERTHS, EACH CAPABLE
OF BUILDING VESSELS 100 FEET WIDE, HAVE BEEN REBUILT
INTO A BERTH WHICH CAN TAKE VESSELS 150 FEET IN WIDTH.
PHOTO SHOWS:
BRITAIN'S FIRST 100,000-TON TANKER
UNDER CONSTRUCTION IN THE VICKERS-ARMSTRONGS YARD
FROM WHERE IT WILL BE LAUNCHED EARLY NEXT YEAR.

activity: Customs official boarding and on deck of an arrested French trawler.

te.text:
SIGHTING a French trawler, Notre Dame de Lourdes, within the three-mile limit off Rye Bay, early yesterday, the British gun-boat Kingfisher went alongside. The trawler moved off and Kingfisher followed her for 20 minutes, calling on her to stop.
Then, as she took no notice, the gun-boat fired a round of blank over her bows. The trawler came to a standstill, and later in the day her master was fined £10, including costs, at Dover, for being within British fishery limits.
The master, John Baptiste Margolle, blamed the flood tide for his being within the limit. All his gear was aboard.
There was no suggestion, said the Kingfisher's commander, that the trawl was down.
Top picture shows a customs official on the deck of the trawler in Dover Harbour; below, the officer is seen boarding the vessel from a customs launch. The gun-boat Kingfisher is in the background.

te.text:
THE TRAGEDY OF BRITAIN'S HARVEST.
FARMERS FIGHT THE WEATHER.         AW/RS

The abnormal rainfall this summer and the absence of a
period of sunny weather to ripen and dry the wheat is
giving the farmers an anxious time - especially now, harvest
time. These pictures, taken today on a farm at Godstone,
Surrey, illustrate just how the weather is interfering
with the harvest. The workers also are losing financially -
they are all volunteers from a harvest holiday camp, and
only get paid when actually working.

Photo shows:-   A picture that tells the story of the [struck through: fight]
struggle to garner the badly needed harvest. Volunteer
workers, wearing the Army capes provided for them, stand
by helpless as the rain further beats down the crops.
Fox August 20th. 46.

THIS PRINT IS THE PROPERTY OF THE
"DAILY HERALD" ART LIBRARY
AND MUST BE RETURNED UNDAMAGED.

Standing by helpless while
rain ruins the crops, these
cape-clad harvesters were
photographed at Godstone,
Surrey. They had been
forced to abandon work
when rain caused the sheaves
to stick in the cutting
machines.

activity: Kenneth Foster, a pipe inspector, examining North Sea gas pipes rusting in a depot at Great Yarmouth.

te.text: Ind - Fuel - Oil from Sea Bed - N. Sea Exps.

DESPITE claims by the tobaccon-
ists, who admittedly were thinking
of something rather different when
they elected actor Andrew Cruick-
shank as Pipeman of the Year last
month, Mr. Kenneth Foster must
be considered a strong contender
for the title.
Mr. Foster is a pipe inspector. As
may be deduced, he inspects pipes. But
the pipes he expertly studies are very
special pipes indeed—35 miles of them,
all intended to carry gas, or oil, from
the North Sea to Britain.
They have to be inspected because
at the moment, all these pipes are
steadily rusting away in a depot at
Great Yarmouth, Norfolk. It is a
process which is likely to continue for
some time—for the time, in fact, it
takes barristers, businessmen, preserv-
ationists and all to argue whether they
should be used to convey gas, or oil, to
a processing plant at Bacton, Norfolk.
A public inquiry begins today and
its machinations will take some time.
Depot officials are fatalistic: 'It
doesn't matter how long they rust
away. We can always brush them up.
And we know they'll be used some-
where.'
In the meantime, Mr. Foster carries
on inspecting. It won't be his fault if
the first North Sea gas (or oil)
pipeline springs a leak.

title: A photographic print of Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip, Visit to Shetlands, August, 1960

activity: Royal visit to the Shetland Islands including a reception in Lerwick.

te.text:
ART LIBRARY
TO
PLEASE RETURN
11 AUG 1960
DAILY HERALD
PROPERTY OF

Shetlanders forgive the Queen
THE roar that greeted the Queen as
she stepped ashore in the Shetland
Islands yesterday told her: "All is for-
given."
Remember the bitter disappointment in
the Shetlands last summer when the
Queen's first-ever visit was cancelled on the
eve of her arrival? The baby was expected.
But the Shetlanders, whose hardy
womenfolk return to the fields 48 hours
after having their babies, are not people to
harbour a grievance.
"Thank you for such a forgiving wel-
come," said the Queen. She, too, remem-
bered the local criticism of her advisers
who were considered "too off-handed."
This was the first visit of a monarch to
the Shetlands since the Viking kings landed
700 years ago.
After the reception in Lerwick, the Queen
in flowerpot hat and loose coat of cyclamen
pink, faced a gale to meet the crofters and
fishermen in their lonely homes strung out
across Shetland.
Joking with the Lerwick lifeboat crew,
Prince Philip was told of their various
"landlubber" trades. He jibed: "I would
not like to go to sea with you lot."
But later he noticed a scroll for valour
on the wall. Every man of that crew had
an award for rescuing a Russian crew in
a midnight gale.
"I take it all back," said Philip.

activity: Theft of a prefab bungalow house in Croydon.

te.text:
DAILY HERALD March 20 1959 5
Stolen—
a house
and all
mod. con.
Herald Reporter
FOUR cheerful young men took a pre-fab bungalow to pieces, loaded it in to a lorry, and drove away.
And that led to the strangest entry that police at Croydon, Surrey, have ever put in their log-book. It reads:
"Stolen; one prefab, with two bedrooms, lounge, kitchen and bathroom, fitted cupboards and all mod. con."
The prefab is — or WAS — in Firtree - avenue, Shrublands, Croydon. It was empty, and had been sold by Croydon council to a man in Suffolk, who was expected to take it away.
But the four young men beat him to it.
'A ROW'
As they worked, unhurriedly, neighbours watched, thinking they were contractors' men.
Mr. Charles Jones, a plasterer, who lives in the next house, said yesterday: "I was an innocent witness to the crime. I had a row with one of the men for flinging bits and pieces into my garden."
Police admit they haven't a clue — not even a finger-print.

activity: Mrs Carol Hammond and her children Gary, Ian and Neal in their 9th floor flat, which they are frequently unable to leave due to broken lifts.

te.text:
ARTHUR STEEL            22.2.66
LIFT TROUBLE IN COUNCIL FLATS
When the lifts in the huge blocks of flats are out of order(and this
oftens happen) old people and mothers with babies are trapped in their
flats as the stairs are unmanageable.
OPS...Mrs Carol Hammond and her children Gary 7, Ian 2 and Neal
10 months are often sealed off in their 9th floor flat in James
Hammett House, Bethnal Green.E.

TWICE a week, and sometimes
more, the world becomes a for-
bidden place for Carol Hammond
and her children. Inaccessible. Un-
attainable. Out of bounds.
Man may send Lunikular things
up to the moon, but the family
cannot even get down to ground
level. And if they could, they
wouldn't get up again.
So they stay put, trapped in their
ninth-floor home—the victims of lifts
which work if you're lucky but don't if
you're not.
The Hammonds are just one of the
families who suffer from liftlessness in
the Dorset Estate flats at Tower
Hamlets, London.
ONE-HOUR CLIMB
There's the woman of 76 who lives on
the 10th floor and needs support when
she walks.
When the lifts give up—"and some-
times they don't get fixed for days"—
her 74-year-old brother climbs up and
down the stairs to go shopping for her.
There's 58-year-old Albert Yeomans
who has asthma and lives on the
eighth floor. Once he took an hour to
climb the stairs.
So now, when he gets home and finds
the lift motionless he goes to his son's
home and sleeps there. Anything but
face those stairs.
Then there's Mrs. Ham-
mond, 28-year-old mother of
three young sons—Garry,
aged seven, Ian, who is two,
and 10-month-old Neal.
She says: "Whenever I want
to take the children out in the
pram I send Garry to make sure
the lift is working.
"If it isn't, I just give up
and stay home. This has hap-
pened too often to count."
The borough council are "dis-
tressed" about the situation.
New lifts have been ordered but
they are not expected for an-
other five months.
The borough's housing officer,
Miss Joan Simpson, said yester-
day: "The lifts do have a
harder life than those in blocks
of offices and luxury flats, be-
cause children tend to play
around with them.
"Tradesmen probably give
them a hard time, too, by jam-
ming the doors open while they
make deliveries. And perhaps
the lifts are simply getting old."

activity: a pipe for women featuring a ring of diamonds set in platinum

te.text:
THIS PHOTOGRAPH IS THE PROPERTY OF
AND MUST BE RETURNED TO THE
"DAILY HERALD"
EDITORIAL ART LIBRARY
27 JUL 1948
UNDAMAGED.

She has a cure for
cigarette shortage
A SCHOOLGIRL has hit
upon an idea to end
the cigarette shortage.
She is Maureen Guerin, of
Silverdale - street, Kemp-
ston, Beds, and she writes to
the Daily Herald:
"I am just going to give you
a schoolgirl's idea of how the
problem of the cigarette short-
age might be solved.
"I have found out for myself
that many of the heaviest
cigarette smokers are women.
Why is this? In many cases it
is because women either dare
not or cannot smoke a pipe.
"Take, for instance, a woman
who dares not smoke a pipe in
public because she feels em-
barrassed. That woman can
only go on smoking her 20 or
30 cigarettes a day.
"Now if ladies' pipes were
designed to look attractive and
dainty, then I believe women
would go as crazy about them
as they did about slacks, which
really came from the men's
trousers."
When told of the idea, a
famous London firm of pipe-
makers said that they already
have a number of pipes at all
prices specially designed for
women (the one you see below
has a ring of diamonds set in
platinum round the stem, and
costs £9 10s.). Three or four
a week are sold.
Manager of another firm said
that he didn't think women
would go to the bother of fill-
ing and cleaning a pipe.
What do women smokers
think?

Bakery is among the large variety of skilled
manual trades, for which courses of training are
now available, for men and womenx now being released
from War Service. The courses of six months
duration and upwards, according to trade chosen

all trainees receive allowances, free of Income
Tax, on completion of training the Ministry of
Labour assists in finding jobs, up to the

and ten other Ex Servicemen began a 17 week
bakery course. Under the instructions of Mr. L.O.
Smith a former, United Kingdom National Diploma
winner, who until Jan. was a Warrant Officer Master
Baker Instructor, in the Army, now demobilies,
he hopes to pass on much of his experience to
ex service colleagues.

Oct 19th 1966 PAP    ST 430-5 (Sa-G)

HARVESTING VITAMINS

The rich vitamin harvest - the bright red
rose hips of the wild English rose - tipped
from the baskets by schoolchildren
who have culled the "fruit" from the
hedgerows at Mitford, near Newcastle.
Left to right - ANNE SAVAGE, 12; MICHAEL
GLADSTONE, 12; IAN DUNS, 12; and LYNN
BOOTH, 13 (all of Seaton Burn County
School, Wideopen, Northumberland.
"Hipping" not only provides good fun,
but is also a source of extra pocket money
for the children. They are paid by the
pound and part of the money received goes
to school funds.
The hips, very rich in Vitamin C, are
turned into health-giving syrup for the young.
Because a colder climate yields a higher
Vitamin C content, the north of England and
parts of Scotland are most popular for the
harvest.

te.text:
① 7 1/2" x 6 1/4" Rule.
3/16" Rule at top
P7 ED

After producing nearly three million tons
of steel the 43 years old 'B' furnace ends
its career.
It is one of 21 open hearth furnaces
at the Rotherham works of Steel, Peech and
Tozer at present producing 5 per cent of
British total steel output, which are being
replaced by six 100 ton electric arc furnaces
which will produce steel quicker and cheaper.
The picture sequence shows the
last working day in the life of the giant

te.text:
MOBILE POWER UNIT FOR VENEZUELAN OILFIELDS

A complete electrical sub-station on wheels -
the first of its kind to be constructed in this
country - is now on its way to Venezuela for use
in Shell's oilfields around Lake Maracaibo.  Being
easily mobile at short notice the sub-station will
augment or temporarily replace any of the existing
14 static sub-stations and can also be used to
provide a temporary supply to parts of the oilfields
not served by permanent stations.  The plant and
all necessary control gear are fixed and cabled up
on a towed 40-ton trailer, with accessories carried
in an accompanying truck.  The unit was constructed
by Messrs. Parolle Electrical Plant Co. Ltd. of
Newcastle-upon-Tyne.

activity: R. Weeks competing in a hop stringing competition at Pattenden Farm.

te.text:
APRIL 9th. 1968.

HOP STRINGING COMPETITION.

          Hop stringers, the name given to men and women
who every year weave the vast "spider's web" of cord
yarn - some 300,000 miles of it - on which will grow
the hops required to flavour the nine thousand million-
odd pints of beer Britons can be expected to drink next
year, had their own competition in Kent today - the
Weald of Kent Ploughing Match Association's annual hop-
stringing competition - held at Pattenden Farm, Marden,
Kent.     The stringers carry the yarn in baskets slung
over their shoulders, and by means of poles, ten feet or
more long and tipped with iron tubing through which the
cord runs, thread it from pegs in the ground to hooks set
on wires 15 1/2 feet above the gardens.    The result is that
from each site of a growing hop plant, called "a hill",
arises a pattern of string resembling the spokes of an
umbrella - the name given to the type of stringing most
frequently met with in the South East.   The stringers,
who in the competition have to "string a cant of about
200 hills", are followed by assistants - usually women -
who act as "banders-in" and tie each group of four vertical
strings together about five feet from the ground.

KEYSTONE PHOTO SHOWS:-      MR. R. WEEKS, a competitor
          in the open class, displays his art at "stringing"
          during the competition today.
